rows.title: Learn what documents you will need to get a Social Security Card | SSASearch
rows.content: Skip to main content An official website of the United States government Here's how you know Official websites use .govA .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States. Secure .gov websites use HTTPSA lock ( ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. ... ... Social Security X Benefits BY PHASE Prepare Apply Manage benefits BY TYPE Retirement Disability Survivor Family Supplemental Security Income (SSI) Benefits overview Medicare Plan for Medicare Sign up for Medicare Request to lower IRMAA Apply for Part D Extra Help Manage Medicare benefits Card & record Number & card Personal record Search Español Sign in Menu Learn what documents you will need to get a Social Security Card (En español) Who is the card for An Adult A Child Type of card Original Replacement Corrected Citizenship of the person the card is for U.S. Born Citizen Foreign Born U.S. Citizen Foreign Born U.S. Citizen - Adopted Noncitizen Corrected Card for a Foreign Born U.S. Citizen Adult If you legally change your name because of marriage, divorce, court order, or any other reason, you need to tell Social Security so that you can get a corrected card. If you are working, you also need to tell your employer. If you do not tell us when your name changes, it may: Prevent your wages from being posted correctly to your Social Security record, which may lower the amount of your future Social Security benefits. Cause delays when you file your taxes. Important You must present original documents or copies certified by the agency that issued them. We cannot accept photocopies or notarized copies. All documents must be current (not expired). We cannot accept a receipt showing you applied for the document. We may use one document for two purposes. For example, we may use your U.S. passport as proof of both citizenship and identity. What original documents do I need? Citizenship If you have not already established your U.S. citizenship with us, we need to see proof of U.S. citizenship. We can accept only certain documents as proof of U.S. citizenship. These include: U.S. passport; Certificate of Naturalization (N-550/N-570); Certificate of Citizenship (N-560/N-561); Certificate of Report of Birth (DS-1350); Consular Report of Birth Abroad (FS-240, CRBA). Important We require this documentation only if you have NOT already established U.S. citizenship with us. Name Change If you need to change your name on your Social Security card, you must show us proof of your legal name change. Documents Social Security may accept to prove a legal name change include: Marriage document; Divorce decree; Certificate of Naturalization showing the new name; or Court order approving the name change. If the document you provide as evidence of a legal name change does not give us enough information to identify you in our records or if you changed your name more than two years ago (four years ago if you are under 18 years of age), you must show us an identity document in your prior name (as shown in our records). We will accept an identity document in your old name that has expired. If you do not have an identity document in your prior name, we may accept an unexpired identity document in your new name as long as we can properly establish your identity in our records. Identity We can accept only certain documents as proof of identity. For example, as proof of identity Social Security must see: U.S. driver's license; State-issued non-driver identification card; or U.S. passport. If you do not have one of these specific documents or you cannot get a replacement for one of them within 10 days, we will ask to see other documents. Any documents submitted, including the following, must be current (not expired) and show your name, identifying information (date of birth or age) and preferably a recent photograph: Employee identification card; School identification card; Health insurance card (not a Medicare card); or U.S. military identification card. Custody and Responsibility Documentation If you are filing on behalf of someone else, in addition to documents to prove your age, identity, and citizenship status. We may ask you to provide documents that show you have custody of, or responsibility for the person for whom you are filing for. Examples of acceptable documents include: Court custody documentation Letter from state social service placing the individual in your household Other documents that show your relationship and responsibility Physical or Mental incapacity Documentation Documentation that the individual is physically or mentally unable to file an application on his or her behalf (e.g. doctor’s certification) Note Your new card will have the same number as your previous card but will show your new name. We will mail your card as soon as we have all of your information and have verified your documents. Correct Information on your Social Security record When applying for a Social Security replacement card online, you have the option to update or correct the information we have about you in our records, such as date of birth, place of birth, one or both of your parents’ names, your citizenship, or your immigration status. We will ask you to bring original documents into a Social Security field office or card center to complete these updates. Correct Date of Birth To correct your date of birth, please provide one of the following documents: Birth certificate U.S. hospital record of birth Religious record established before age 5 showing age or date of birth Valid passport Final adoption decree showing the information was taken from the original birth certificate Tribal identification card Correct Place of Birth To correct your place of birth, please provide one of the following documents: Birth certificate U.S. passport or passport card Federal or state census record Foreign birth certificate Religious record established before age 5 showing age or date of birth Correct Parent’s Name To correct one or both of your parents’ names, please provide one of the following documents: Birth certificate with the correct name Final adoption decree Court determination of paternity Foreign passport Correct Citizenship or Immigration Status To correct proof of your citizenship or immigration status, please provide one of the following documents: Citizenship U.S. passport Certificate of Naturalization (N-550) Immigration status Permanent Resident Card (I-551), Green Card Employment Authorization Document (I-766), work permit Other Social Security Number Issues Not Previously Listed Schedule an in-office appointment at Make or change an appointment; or Call 1-800-772-1213 Note These updates to your record will not appear on your Social Security card. Corrected Card for a Noncitizen Adult If you change your name, become a U.S. citizen, or your immigration status or work authorization has changed, you need to tell Social Security so we can update our records and when necessary, issue a new card. When you request a replacement or a corrected Social Security card, you must show us proof of your identity, immigration status and work authorization. In addition, if you need to change or correct any information on your Social Security card, you need to show us certain documents about the change. We can only accept certain documents. What documents do I need to prove my identity? Social Security will ask to see your current U.S. immigration documents. Acceptable documents include: I-551 Permanent Resident Card I-94 Arrival/Departure Record with unexpired foreign passport, or admission stamp in the unexpired foreign passport; or I-766 Employment Authorization Document, (EAD, work permit) from DHS. Important You must present original documents or copies certified by the agency that issued them. We cannot accept photocopies or notarized copies. All documents must be current (not expired). We cannot accept a receipt showing you applied for the document. We may use one document for two purposes. For example, we may use your U.S. passport as proof of both citizenship and identity. Custody and Responsibility Documentation If you are filing on behalf of someone else, in addition to documents to prove your age, identity, and citizenship status. We may ask you to provide documents that show you have custody of, or responsibility for, the person for whom you are filing for. Examples of acceptable documents include: Court custody documentation Letter from state social service placing the individual in your household Other documents that show your relationship and responsibility Physical or Mental incapacity Documentation Documentation that the individual is physically or mentally unable to file an application on his or her behalf (e.g. doctor’s certification) What other documents do I need? Name Change If you legally change your name because of marriage, divorce, court order, or any other reason, you should tell Social Security. If you are working, you also need to tell your employer. If you do not tell us when your name changes, it may: Prevent your wages from being posted correctly to your Social Security record, which may lower the amount of your future Social Security benefits. Cause delays when you file your taxes. You must show us proof of your legal name change. Documents Social Security may accept to prove a legal name change include: Marriage document; Divorce decree; Court order approving the name change; or If the document you provide as evidence of a legal name change does not give us enough information to identify you in our records or if you changed your name more than two years ago (four years ago if you are under 18 years of age), you must show us an identity document in your prior name (as shown in our records). We will accept an identity document in your old name that has expired. If you do not have an identity document in your prior name, we may accept an unexpired identity document in your new name, as long as we can properly establish your identity in our records. If we assigned you a Social Security number for non-work purposes, special rules apply. If DHS did not authorize you to work, we will change your name on our records but we cannot issue you a corrected card. If you do not have permission to work, but need a Social Security card for other reasons, see "If you do not have permission to work" for further information. Remember that you cannot use a Social Security number assigned for non-work purposes to work. If you use it to work, we will inform DHS. Note If we issue you a new card, it will have the same number as your previous card, but will show your new name. We will mail your card as soon as we have all of your information and have verified your immigration documents. Immigration Status To prove your U.S. immigration status, you must show us your current U.S. immigration document, such as: Form I-551 (Lawful Permanent Resident Card, Machine Readable Immigrant Visa); I-766 (Employment Authorization Document, EAD, work permit); or I-94 (Arrival/Departure Record) or admission stamp in the unexpired foreign passport. If you are an F-1 or M-1 student, you also must show us your I-20 (Certificate of Eligibility for Nonimmigrant Student Status). If you are a J-1 or J-2 exchange visitor, you must show us your DS-2019 (Certificate of Eligibility for Exchange Visitor Status). Work Eligibility In general, only noncitizens who have DHS' permission to work can apply for a Social Security number. If you are a foreign worker, we only need to see your I-94 (Arrival/Departure Record) or admission stamp in your unexpired foreign passport showing a class of admission permitting work. You may need to show your I-766 (Employment Authorization Document, EAD, work permit) from DHS. If you are lawfully present in the United States and plan to apply for work authorization, you can apply for both work authorization from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) and request a Social Security card from the Social Security Administration at the same time. For more information on this process, read “Apply For Your Social Security Number While Applying For Your Work Permit”. If you submit evidence of lawful work-authorized status along with evidence of your name change, we can issue you a corrected card with your new name. Student: F-1 If you are an F-1 student and eligible to work on campus, you must provide a letter from your designated school official that: Identifies you; Confirms your current school status; and Identifies your employer and the type of work you are, or will be, doing. We also need to see evidence of that employment, such as a recent pay slip or a letter from your employer. Your supervisor must sign and date the letter. The letter must describe: Your job; Your employment start date; The number of hours you are, or will be, working; and Your supervisor's name and telephone number. If you are an F-1 student authorized to work in curricular practical training, you must provide us your Form I-20 with the employment page completed and signed by your designated school official. If you are an F-1 student and have a work permit (I-766) from DHS, you must present it. J-1 If you are a J-1 student, student intern or international visitor, you must provide a letter from your sponsor. The letter should be on sponsor letterhead with an original signature that authorizes your employment. If you do not have permission to work: Lawfully admitted noncitizens can get many benefits and services without a Social Security number. You do not need a number to conduct business with a bank, register for school, apply for educational tests, obtain private health insurance, apply for school lunch programs or apply for subsidized housing. You cannot get a Social Security number for the sole purpose of obtaining a driver's license. Citizenship If you have not already established your U.S. citizenship with us, we need to see proof of U.S. citizenship. We can accept only certain documents as proof of U.S. citizenship. These include: U.S. passport; Certificate of Naturalization (N-550/N-570); Certificate of Citizenship (N-560/N-561); Certificate of Report of Birth (DS-1350); Consular Report of Birth Abroad (FS-240, CRBA). Important We require citizenship documentation only if you are a U.S. citizen and you have NOT already established U.S. citizenship with us. Correct Information on your Social Security record When applying for a Social Security replacement card online, you have the option to update or correct the information we have about you in our records, such as date of birth, place of birth, one or both of your parents’ names, your citizenship, or your immigration status. We will ask you to bring original documents into a Social Security field office or card center to complete these updates. Correct Date of Birth To correct your date of birth, please provide one of the following documents: Birth certificate U.S. hospital record of birth Religious record established before age 5 showing age or date of birth Valid passport Final adoption decree showing the information was taken from the original birth certificate Tribal identification card Correct Place of Birth To correct your place of birth, please provide one of the following documents: Birth certificate U.S. passport or passport card Federal or state census record Foreign birth certificate Religious record established before age 5 showing age or date of birth Correct Parent’s Name To correct one or both of your parents’ names, please provide one of the following documents: Birth certificate with the correct name Final adoption decree Court determination of paternity Foreign passport Correct Citizenship or Immigration Status To correct proof of your citizenship or immigration status, please provide one of the following documents: Citizenship U.S. passport Certificate of Naturalization (N-550) Immigration status Permanent Resident Card (I-551), Green Card Employment Authorization Document (I-766), work permit Other Social Security Number Issues Not Previously Listed Schedule an in-office appointment at Make or change an appointment; or Call 1-800-772-1213 Note These updates to your record will not appear on your Social Security card. Corrected Card for a U.S. Born Adult If you legally change your name because of marriage, divorce, court order or any other reason, you need to tell Social Security so that you can get a corrected card. If you are working, also tell your employer. If you do not tell us when your name changes, it may: Prevent your wages from being posted correctly to your Social Security record, which may lower the amount of your future Social Security benefits. Cause delays when you file your taxes. Important We cannot accept photocopies or notarized copies. We cannot accept a receipt showing you applied for the document. All documents must be current (not expired). We may use one document for two purposes. For example, we may use your U.S. passport as proof of both citizenship and identity. What original documents do I need? Citizenship If you have not already established your U.S. citizenship with us, we need to see proof of U.S. citizenship. We can accept only certain documents as proof of U.S. citizenship. These include a U.S. birth certificate or U.S. passport. Important This documentation is only required if you have NOT already established citizenship with us. Name change If you need to change your name on your Social Security card, you must show us proof of your legal name change. Documents Social Security may accept to prove a legal name change include: Marriage document; Divorce decree; Certificate of Naturalization showing the new name; or Court order approving the name change. If the document you provide as evidence of a legal name change does not give us enough information to identify you in our records or if you changed your name more than two years ago (four years ago if you are under 18 years of age), you must show us an identity document in your prior name (as shown in our records). We will accept an identity document in your old name that has expired. If you do not have an identity document in your prior name, we may accept an unexpired identity document in your new name, as long as we can properly establish your identity in our records. Identity We can accept only certain documents as proof of identity. An acceptable document must be current (not expired) and show your name, identifying information (date of birth or age) and preferably a recent photograph. For example, as proof of identity Social Security must see your: U.S. driver's license; State-issued non-driver identification card; or U.S. passport. If you do not have one of these specific documents or you cannot get a replacement for one of them within 10 days, we will ask to see other documents. Any documents submitted, including the following, must be current (not expired) and show your name, identifying information (date of birth or age) and preferably a recent photograph: Employee identification card; School identification card; Health insurance card (not a Medicare card); or U.S. military identification card. Custody and Responsibility Documentation If you are filing on behalf of someone else (an adult or a child), in addition to documents to prove your age, identity, and citizenship status. We may ask you to provide documents that show you have custody of, or responsibility for, the person you are filing for. Examples of acceptable documents include: Court custody documentation Letter from state social service placing the individual in your household Other documents that show your relationship and responsibility Physical or Mental incapacity Documentation Documentation that the individual is physically or mentally unable to file an application on his or her behalf (e.g. doctor’s certification) Note Your new card

Contact You are here: VGF Tickets, Fares & Plans Tickets & Purchase Overview of RMV tickets Category Category Show all Single tickets Day tickets Season tickets Major- and company customers Deutschland-TicketTravel all day on local and regional transport throughout Germany for 63 euros per month. The ticket can be cancelled monthly. It is not transferable to another person. More Buy ticket online Deutschland-Ticket (Hessenpass mobil) for people from HessenSame conditions as the Deutschland-Ticket, but available at a reduced price of 44 euros per month with proof of Hessenpass mobil. The place of residence must be in Hesse. More Buy ticket online Deutschland-Ticket (Hessenpass mobil) Same conditions as the Deutschland-Ticket, but available at a reduced price of 31.50 euros per month with proof of Hessenpass mobil and Frankfurt-Pass. The place of residence must be in Frankfurt. More Buy ticket online School pupils and vocational traineesThe RMV Schülerticket Hesse for any number of journeys throughout Hesse. Available for 33.80 euros per month or a one-off 398 euros for one year. Even cheaper with proof of Frankfurt-Pass. More Buy ticket online Over 65 yearsThe RMV-Seniorenticket Hessen for any number of journeys throughout Hessen. Available for 33.80 euros per month or a one-off 398 euros for one year. Even cheaper with proof of Frankfurt-Pass. More Buy ticket online Deutschland-Ticket (Frankfurt-Pass mobil)Same conditions as the Deutschland-Ticket, but available at a reduced rate of 31.50 euros per month with proof of Frankfurt-Pass mobil. The place of residence must be in Frankfurt. More Buy ticket online Weekly Ticket (Wochenkarte)Available for adults and children at any price level (including transitional fares) and valid for seven consecutive days. From 5 days, already cheaper than RMV day tickets of the same price level. More Monthly Ticket (Monatskarte)Available for adults and children at any fare level (including transitional fares) and valid until the same date in the following month. Discounted with proof of Frankfurt Pass. More Annual Ticket (Jahreskarte)Available for adults and children at any price level (including the transition tariff). Can be paid monthly or for an entire year. More Buy ticket online Tickets with Frankfurt-PassThe Deutschland Ticket, RMV Schülerticket Hessen, RMV Seniorenticket Hessen or the RMV monthly travelcard at a reduced price with proof of Frankfurt Pass. More Buy ticket online JobTicketTravel to work and in your free time by bus and train at low cost. Employers can buy the RMV-JobTicket and the Deutschland-Ticket Job for their employees and subsidise them flexibly. More StudentsThe RMV Semesterticket is available to all students who are enrolled at a university in the RMV area. The ticket is issued by the university. More Single TicketRMV Ticket for one journey (without return journey, round trip, longer interruptions or detours). Can be purchased directly before travelling for adults and children aged 6 and over. More Short Trip TicketRMV Single ticket for short journeys. Whether the destination is a short-distance journey is indicated on notices at the bus stop or at the ticket machine. More Connection TicketThe supplement to an existing RMV season ticket if you wish to travel beyond your area of validity. More Single Add-on Ticket (1st class)For journeys in 1st class in conjunction with an existing RMV ticket (single journey, annual or other season tickets). Otherwise, the same rules apply as for single tickets. More Day TicketsAvailable for adults and children in every fare category (including transitional fares). For any number of journeys on the day of validity until 5 a.m. on the following day. Cheaper than a RMV single ticket of the same price level for 2 or more journeys. More Group Day TicketValid for up to 5 people and can be cheaper than individual RMV day tickets from the 2nd person. Not transferable, as the names must be entered on the RMV ticket. More Large Group TicketValid for 10 people and is up to 40 per cent cheaper than sRMV ingle tickets. Otherwise, the same rules apply as for the RMV day ticket. More HessenTicketFor 1 to 5 people throughout Hesse on local and regional transport. Valid on weekdays from 9 a.m., all day on weekends and public holidays. More Frankfurt CardFor 1 to 5 people on local and regional transport in the entire Frankfurt city area, including the airport. Not transferable to other persons. Also offers discounts on tours, round trips and much more. More RhineMainCardFor 1 to 5 people on local and regional transport throughout the RMV network. Not transferable to other persons. Offers additional discounts at many leisure destinations. More Hotel Guest Ticket (HotelgastTicket)An offer for youth hostels and hotels in Frankfurt and the surrounding area. Hotel guests can enquire about this offer at the reception of their booked hotel or youth hostel. More ServiceTicketAn offer for service garages for customers who have to hand in their vehicle for repair. Available as a day pass for the Frankfurt city area. More TourTicketAn offer for organisers of large events (100 participants or more), such as conferences or congresses in Frankfurt. The validity of the tickets can be customised. More CombiTicketAn offer for organisers of major events such as concerts, sporting events and trade fairs. The temporal and spatial validity of the tickets can be customised. More CongressTicketAn offer for organisers of congresses and conferences. Entitles event participants to any number of journeys on one or two days in the Frankfurt city area, including the airport. rows.title: Best Neighbourhoods in London for Expats | 2025 Guide
rows.content: stay@thesqua.re+44 (0) 203-701-30103, Barrel Yard, Vinery Way, London W6 0LQWhereCheck InCheck OutWhoBest Neighbourhoods in London for ExpatsHomeRelocation GuidesMoving to London GuideAccommodationBest Neighbourhoods in London & Accommodation Guide for Expats London is one of the world's most thrilling cities, but also, perhaps, one of the most nuanced for deciding where to call home. With more than 8 million inhabitants and hundreds of individual neighborhoods, expats frequently wonder: "Where do I live in London?" You're making the move on your own, or with your significant other, or with your family in tow. The right London neighbourhood makes all the difference. Where to Live in London as an Expat London has been divided into various zones, each with its own flavor, budget, and way of living. As a London expat, your choice is usually based on: Commute: Being close to your workplace or business districts, such as the City and Canary Wharf. Lifestyle: Family-friendly suburbs and quiet living, or is nightlife for you? Budget: Typical rents range greatly by neighborhood, from £1,800 a month in East London to £6,000+ in Central London. Community: Most expats — particularly American expats in London — opt for neighborhoods with international schools and settled expat communities. Best Neighbourhoods in London for Expats 1. Central London: Prestige & Convenience Neighborhoods in demand: Kensington, Chelsea, Marylebone, Mayfair. Why expats opt for it: Walking distance from offices, world-class restaurants, luxury flats. Best for: Professionals and executives looking for an upscale lifestyle. Rent guide: £2,500–£4,500 per month for a 1–2 bedroom apartment. 2. West London: Family-Friendly Living Hot areas: Notting Hill, Chiswick, Fulham, Richmond. Why expats prefer it: Green streets, international schools, parks. Regarded as among the finest London neighborhoods for expats with families. Best for: Couples and families moving long-term. Rent guide: £2,000–£3,500 per month for a family house. 3. North London: Village Atmosphere & Schools Most popular areas: Hampstead, Highgate, Islington, Camden. Why expats prefer it: Village-like atmosphere with cultural hubs and high-quality schools. Best for: Professionals and families seeking room with convenient access to the City. Rent guide: £2,500–£4,000 per month for family properties. 4. East London: Trendy & Modern Neighbourhoods Most popular areas: Shoreditch, Canary Wharf, Stratford, Hackney. Why expats prefer it: Finance and technology centers, trendy flats, and nightlife. Best for: Young professionals and singles. Rent guide: £1,800–£3,000 per month for new-build flats. 5. South London: Space & Suburban Comfort Popular areas: Clapham, Wimbledon, Dulwich, Greenwich. Why expats choose it: Bigger houses, extra space, family neighborhoods. A favorite among US expats living in London for its suburban lifestyle. Best for: Families looking for affordability and parks. Rent guide: £2,000–£3,500 per month for family houses. Good Neighbourhoods in London for Expats If you’re looking for recommendations by lifestyle: For Families: Richmond, Dulwich, Hampstead, Wimbledon. For Young Professionals: Shoreditch, Canary Wharf, Islington. For American Expats: Kensington, Chelsea, Notting Hill (due to international schools and established expat communities). Accommodation Options in London When it comes to housing, expats can choose from a variety of accommodation types: 1. Serviced Apartments in London Fully furnished, flexible rentals, perfect for executives relocating short-term or those who want a stress-free start. Utilities and cleaning are often included. 2. Private Rentals Standard long-term leases (typically 12 months) where you’ll furnish the property yourself. Popular with couples and families staying longer. 3. Luxury Apartments High-end complexes in Central and Canary Wharf with concierge, gyms, and city views. These are popular with business executives and expats residing in London looking for comfort and convenience. 4. Family Homes West, North, and South London offer spacious family homes, typically with gardens, located close to parks and schools, an attractive option for expats with children. Guide to London Neighbourhoods for Expats Choosing where to live in London is about balancing budget, lifestyle, and commute. While the city can feel overwhelming at first, the right area will make it feel like home. That’s why we’ve created a Comprehensive Guide to London Neighbourhoods, with detailed cost breakdowns, schooling options, transport links, and insider tips for expats. [Download the guide now] to discover the ideal neighbourhood for your way of life and make your move to London seamless.RELOCATION GUIDE CHAPTERS Visa & Immigration Cost of Living in London Best Neighborhood & Accommodation Know Your Rights in London Banking, Finance & Tax System Getting Around London Tourist Attractions of London Healthcare System in London Education and Schooling Settling In London Follow UsFAQWhere Should I Live in London as an Expat?Where should I live in London as an American expat?Where do most expats live in London?What is a good neighbourhood in London for families?Where should I live in London as a young professional?Download Your Essential Moving to London GuideMoving doesn’t have to feel overwhelming. rows.title: Best areas and suburbs in Dublin | Expat Arrivals
rows.content: Skip to main content Main navigation Home Forum Guides Social Search User account menu Register Log in Breadcrumb Home Europe Ireland Dublin Areas and suburbs in Dublin MovingPros and Cons of MovingCost of LivingGetting AroundHealthcareFrequently Asked QuestionsWeatherWorkingAccommodationAreas and SuburbsShipping and RemovalsSchoolsInternational SchoolsLifestyleKids and FamilySport and FitnessWeekend BreaksCountry infoPros and Cons of MovingDoing BusinessSchoolsAccommodationMoney and TaxesHealthcareLocal CultureCost of Living Download our Moving to Dublin Guide (PDF) The best places to live in DublinAs with all cities, the area in Dublin that you choose to live in can completely change your lifestyle. From the laid-back beaches in North Dublin to the hustle and bustle of city-centre living, there are many diverse areas for you to pick from.When deciding where to settle in Dublin, you should consider the area's proximity to your workplace, good schools and public transport. Traffic is surprisingly heavy for such a small city and commutes of an hour or more both ways are not unheard of.While popular areas like Seapoint, Killiney, Ranelagh and Clontarf are well-known, you might also consider The Liberties, Stoneybatter, Phibsborough and Drumcondra. These areas offer unique atmospheres, from historic charm to trendy, up-and-coming vibes.Dublin has also seen significant changes recently. Increased diversity has brought new cultures and cuisines to the city. As a hub for tech and innovation, Dublin attracts young professionals. Sustainability efforts promote cycling, public transport and green spaces. However, housing costs have risen, making city-centre living a challenge.Below are some of the best areas and suburbs in Dublin. Seaside areas in DublinSeapointSeapoint Beach is a fantastic place to live. It’s perfect for swimming and has the historic Martello Tower, offering great views. The area tends to be pricier than the city centre, but there are beautifully restored Georgian properties if you prefer to rent a house rather than an apartment. The DART service connects you conveniently to central Dublin every 15 to 20 minutes during peak hours.One benefit of living close to the beach is being able to walk or swim every morning. On Sundays, enjoy regular community events like the Dún Laoghaire Harbour Festival and the Dún Laoghaire Market.KillineyKilliney offers stunning natural scenery, with Killiney Hill Park providing vistas of Bray Head, the Wicklow Mountains and Dublin Bay. Killiney Beach curves inward with dramatic peaks of the Sugarloaf Mountains in the background. It’s a more expensive area, but you’ll find beautifully restored Georgian homes. The DART service connects Killiney to central Dublin, making commuting easier.Living here means you can enjoy the picturesque setting and vibrant community, though at a higher cost than other parts of Dublin. Participate in activities like walking along the Dún Laoghaire pier and attending local markets.HowthHowth marks the beginning of the northern beaches. It’s a beautiful area with a strong sense of community. The DART service, which runs every 15 to 20 minutes during peak hours, connects Howth to central Dublin. It’s a great place to live if you enjoy outdoor activities and the seaside atmosphere.Howth offers a range of activities, including sailing, swimming and walking along the seafront. It’s a safe area, but be cautious of slippery rocks and always lock your vehicle when visiting the beach.MalahideMalahide is another excellent seaside area with a welcoming community. The DART service provides easy access to central Dublin every 15 to 20 minutes during peak hours. Malahide is known for its beautiful coastline and vibrant community events.Enjoy activities like sailing, walking along the pier and attending local festivals. The area is generally safe, but it’s always wise to be aware of your surroundings, especially at night.Upmarket suburbs in DublinRanelaghLocated on the south side, Ranelagh is a favourite among expats. It’s just 10 minutes from the city centre and has exceptional public transport links. The area boasts a lively nightlife, with plenty of bars and restaurants. The houses here are beautiful, spacious and perfect if you want a garden, parking and privacy.ClontarfClontarf, situated on the north side, is another popular choice. Like Ranelagh, it’s close to the city centre and offers good public transport. Clontarf has a more relaxed vibe with a strong community feel. The nightlife is lively, and there are beautiful houses with ample space for families.BallsbridgeBallsbridge caters to a more settled crowd. It’s home to many embassies and exudes an upscale, sophisticated atmosphere. With its location near the picturesque River Liffey, Ballsbridge is known for its elegant houses and green spaces. It’s a bit quieter but offers a high standard of living. Thanks to the abundance of restaurants, cafés, and high-end boutiques, it's easy to find something to do without leaving the neighbourhood. DonnybrookDonnybrook, close to Ballsbridge, is another upmarket suburb. It has a similar ambience to Ballsbridge with high-end homes and a more tranquil setting. Yet, the closer you get to Baggot Street, the livelier it becomes. It’s perfect if you want peace and proximity to city life.City life in Central DublinSmithfieldSmithfield has become one of Dublin's most desirable areas over the last decade. It's currently undergoing significant development, including the revitalisation of Smithfield Square and the conversion of The Chocolate Factory into a mixed-use space. These projects enhance the area's charm and functionality.Renting in Smithfield can be pricey, higher than in some other central areas but less than places like Ballsbridge. The variety of shops and services is impressive, from independent boutiques and high-street brands to vibrant restaurants, cafés and bars.The Light House Cinema is a local favourite, known for its cosy, intimate setting and eclectic film selection. Special events add to its appeal, including film festivals and Q&A sessions with filmmakers.The Luas tram line ensures efficient and convenient travel. Trams run every four to six minutes during peak hours and every 10 minutes off-peak. The network connects seamlessly with other public transport services, making commuting around Dublin straightforward. Areas in Dublin to avoidWhile Dublin is generally considered safe, some areas have higher crime rates where extra caution is advised. Ballymun is one such area, known for drug-related violence, gang activity and vandalism. Tallaght also has a reputation for being one of the more dangerous parts of the city, with over 100,000 crimes recorded between 2003 and 2019. Both areas are best avoided, especially at night.Pearse Street and Blanchardstown are other high-crime areas. The North Inner City and South Inner City have certain parts with higher crime rates, particularly in less crowded or poorly lit locations, and staying in well-populated and well-lit areas is advisable. Sheriff Street has historically had issues with drug abuse and gang activity, making it another area where caution is necessary.Despite the higher crime rates in these areas, efforts are underway to improve safety through community development and regeneration projects. Always stay informed about current conditions and exercise caution when necessary. Overall, Dublin remains a vibrant and generally safe city, but awareness of these higher-risk areas can help ensure a safer experience.Which areas and suburbs do expats recommend in Dublin?"In Dublin, it really depends on what housing you can afford. The North is slightly more affordable, but many people would consider it as being a bit more on the “rough” side of the city. If you’re willing to commute into town, Portmarnock and Malahide are lovely seaside areas. In town itself, Dublin 8, Castleknock, Rathfarnham and Rathmines are popular. To the south of Dublin, there are plenty of lovely areas with lots of parks, greenery, and little seaside spots to live in. Dundrum, Cabinteely, Stillorgan, Dún Laoghaire and further out Bray (into the next county) are all great." Read our interview with South African expat Caro to learn more about living in Dublin. rows.title: The right to a doctor in Norway - Helsenorge
rows.content: About General Practitioner on Helsenorge Språk/LanguageNorskEnglish The right to a doctor All inhabitants who are registered in the National Population Register as living in Norway have the right to a General Practitioner/family doctor. The GP situation The GP situation: It is the municipality that is responsible for ensuring that you receive GP services. Some muncipalities in Norway do not have enough GPs. When you have lost your GP: If you have lost your GP and have been moved to a list without a permanent GP, you are still affiliated with a doctor’s surgery. This will often be the doctor’s surgery where you had your GP. Don’t leave it to the last minute: It may be wise to contact the doctor’s surgery well in advance to have your prescriptions renewed, etc. Who is entitled to a General Practitioner? ​Everyone who is registered in the National Population Register as a resident in a Norwegian municipality is entitled to have a General Practitioner (GP; "fastlege" in Norwegian). The municipality is responsible for ensuring that you are offered the necessary general practitioner services. You can also choose a GP in a different municipality to the one you live in. If the municipality you live in has a major shortage of GPs, it may be easier to find a GP with vacancies in a neighbouring municipality. Persons who have D-numbers are not entitled to a GP, the only exceptions are the following groups, who are entitled to a GP: Asylum seekers with D-numbers, and their families NATO personnel with D-numbers and their families Foreign personnel sent as representatives to Norway and their families A D-number is an identity number assigned to people who do not meet the criteria for a standard Norwegian national identification number. Other persons with a D-number are not entitled to a GP, but are entitled necessary medical treatment. The municipality is responsible to providing this kind of healthcare. If you move to another municipality within Norway and later move back to your original municipality within three years, you may be reassigned to your original GP if you register this move in the National Population Register within 6 months. If you are unsure whether you are entitled to a GP, call the user service (Veiledning helsenorge.no) at +47 23 32 70 00. When your GP cancels or reduces their patient list It is the municipality that is responsible for ensuring that you are offered the necessary general practitioner services. If your GP leaves their practice, you will be transferred to another GP’s list. If you are transferred to a list without a specific GP, it will often be a substitute doctor who takes over the responsibility, or it may be another doctor from that practice. In some cases, you may need to use the out-of-hours medical services or immediate assistance to get the necessary medical help. When a GP decides to reduce the number of patients on their list, the selection of patients to be transferred to another list is random by a computer system. Neither the GP nor any other person has the right to decide who shall be transferred and who shall remain on the list. Section 35 of the Regulation relating to a municipal regular GP scheme (only in Norwegian) specifies that a GP’s list shall be reduced through a random selection. Families that are registered at the same address are kept together in the event of such a list reduction. General Practitioner for children under the age of 16 Children under the age of 16 automatically get the same GP as their mother, assuming the parents have joint parental responsibility and share the same address. The parents also have the opportunity to change the child's GP so that the child gets the father's GP. When the parents have joint parental responsibility, the child has the right to the same GP as either the father or the mother. In the case of shared custody, the child will have the same GP as the parent with whom they live. Your child has the right to have the same GP as you, even when your GP does not have a place on the list. You may choose a different GP than your own for your child. Your child does not automatically change GP when you do. You have the right to change GP for your own children who are under the age of 16. This also applies with shared custody of children. In the case of shared custody and joint parental responsibility, the parent who does not live at the same registered address as the child must document parental responsibility. Documentation can be downloaded from skatteetaten.no and sent to Helfo. GPs for children in foster care It is the Child Welfare Service that has the right to change the GP for children living in foster care. Foster parents cannot change the GP for their foster children unless they have authorization from the Child Welfare Service to do so, and the authorization has been sent to Helfo. Children in foster care also do not have the right to change to their foster parents' doctor. GPs for asylum seekers If you have received a registration certificate as an asylum seeker, and you know the municipality where you will be living, you can be assigned a GP. If you are living in an asylum centre, the centre will help you send the necessary documentation to Helfo so that you can be assigned a GP. If you have a private residence, you must send your valid registration certificate as an asylum seeker yourself or with the help of others, in addition to a completed form on the assignment of a GP for asylum seekers with private residence, to Helfo. If you have a GP and wish to change to another GP, you must also send a valid registration certificate to Helfo. The registration certificate is valid for six months. Assigning a General Practitioner for asylum seeker living privately (05-04.31) English (pdf)Tildeling av fastlege for asylsøkar som bur privat (05-04.31) Nynorsk (pdf)Tildeling av fastlege for asylsøkere som bor privat (05-04.31) Bokmål (pdf) A regular GP for persons who have been sent to Norway as foreign representatives The term foreign representatives covers persons who work at embassies, consulates and intergovernmental organisations. Persons sent to Norway as foreign representatives are not automatically assigned a regular GP. This also applies to any family members who join such representatives in Norway. It is optional to enrol in the GP scheme. Your representatives will help you enrol. If you, at a later date, wish to change to a different GP, you will have to call Guidance helsenorge.no on telephone number +47 23 32 70 00. If you have Bank-ID, you can also log in to Helsenorge and change your general practitioner yourself. Having a General Practitioner while you are a student ​GPs associated with the health service at universities and colleges can be used by students who have paid their semester fees, as well as by their children under 16. Students who move back to their former municipality within three years, are entitled to return to their original GP if they register this move in the National Population Register within 6 months, even if the GP's list is full. Students who have formally moved abroad are not entitled to return to their former GP. Are you student connected to the student welfare organization in Oslo, SiO? Read more at SiO's own website. Having a General Practitioner while in a nursing home When staying in a nursing home, you are entitled to keep your regular GP, but you need to use the nursing home doctor while living there. If you want to opt out of or into the general practitioner scheme, you must contact Helsenorge Guidance at phone number 23 32 70 00. General Practitioner assistance in the event of acute illness In the event of acute injury or illness outside of the GP's opening hours, you must contact the out-of-hours medical services, legevakten (116 117). In life-threatening emergency, call 113. ​GPs are responsible for all general medical service for their patients during opening hours. GPs will prioritise patients on their patient list over others, except in the case of acute, life-threatening illness. Out-of-hours medical service Call 116 117 to contact the out-of-hours medical services for your area. Responsibility for the General Practitioner scheme The municipalities manage the General Practitioner scheme and sign agreements with individual GPs. It is the responsibility of each municipality to ensure that there are enough GPs. Each municipality has a supervisor of GPs. This is generally the municipal doctor. Your GP can delegate consultations to a nurse Your GP can delegate consultations to a nurse at their office, if the office has a nurse working there. This means that you can meet a nurse, instead of your GP when you are there for your consultation. If this is the case, you will get information about it. Your GP is still medically responsible regarding your case, and the nurse are required to have the necessary competence. To find out if your GPs office have a nurse available, see the page Bytte fastlege (change GP). Complaints about your GP or the GP scheme ​If you are dissatisfied with your General Practitioner, you are entitled to submit a complaint. Patient dissatisfaction with their GP is often due to communication problems. A useful first step may be to book an appointment with the GP to explain why you are unhappy. You may wish to bring someone along with you for support. When booking the appointment, it is best to notify the GP that you wish to complain. This allows the doctor to reserve more time for the discussion. If you still feel the need to make a complaint, you can consult the person within the municipality who is responsible for the GP scheme (usually the head of health and care services) or send a complaint to the County Medical Officer (fylkeslege), with a copy to the chief municipal doctor (kommuneoverlege). The municipality is responsible for the provision of GPs. If there are no GPs available in the municipality, you can complain to the municipal health department (chief municipal doctor). Opting out of the General Practitioner scheme To manage your registration with the GP scheme, call Guidance helsenorge.no (Veiledning helsenorge.no) at +47 23 32 70 00. What is Universal Health Protection (Puma)?Verified 13 May 2026 - Public Service / Directorate of Legal and Administrative Information (Prime Minister)Financial contribution for some Puma beneficiariesThe Law of 30 December 2025 on the financing of Social Security for 2026 provides for the introduction of a financial contribution for Puma beneficiaries who fulfill three conditions:Reside in France in a stable and regularBeing without professional activityNot be liable for the CSG: titleContent , the CRDS: titleContent and health insurance contributions under an international convention.A decree is expected to be issued on the amount of this financial contribution.An update of this page will be made when the decree is published.In the meantime, the information presented on this page remains valid.Universal health protection (Puma) allows health care costs to be covered without disruption of rights. This means that this care is provided even in the event of a change in professional, family or residence situation. To qualify for the Puma, you must work or reside in France on a stable or regular basis. We present you the information to know. Unfold all What is the objective of the Puma?If you work or reside in France on a stable and regular basis, the Puma guarantees you a right to cover your health costs, in your personal capacity and on an ongoing basis throughout your life.The Puma also allows you to stay in the same health insurance plan, including in the event of a change in employment status (e.g. loss of employment) or personal status (e.g. separation).Any periods of breach of your rights are thus avoided.Who is affected by the Puma?You are affected by the Puma if you work or reside in France on a stable and regular basis.Unlike a minor, if you are of age, there is no need to be attached to an insured person.MajorMinorMajorYou are of full age without professional activity, you have the right to be covered by your health care costs in a personal capacity.There is no need to be attached to a qualifying insured. Indeed, an adult can no longer be entitled since the establishment of the Puma.You are insured individually as soon as you reach the age of majority.You can choose to:Collect refunds on your own bank accountReceive your own refund statementHave your own Ameli account.Thus, you benefit from a better confidentiality of the information on the health costs covered.MinorIf you are a minor, you continue to have the status of a right holder. In practice, you are attached to one of your parents.However, it is possible to apply for Puma in a personal capacity from the age of 16.FYI This status of right holder ends the year you turn 18.What are the conditions related to residence in France to have Puma?There are 2 conditions related to the regularity of the residence and the stability of the residence. These 2 conditions are cumulative.Regularity of residenceBy being national of the European Economic Area and Switzerland, you have the right to move and reside freely in France. An ID or passport is enough.However, if you are a national of another country, you must have a residence permit or document.Stability of the residenceThis criterion will depend on whether or not you are working:Répondez aux questions successives et les réponses s’afficheront automatiquementExercise of a professional activityIf you work and your Puma application is accepted, you are immediately enrolled in the Health Insurance.Without the exercise of a professional activityOnce in France, you must wait 3 months before seeing your rights open.These rights remain open if you live in France for at least 6 months of the year.Warning This condition of stability of the residence (3 months) is met without delay for some people. Examples: refugees, people returning to France after a international volunteering abroad, persons who perceive theDisabled Adult Allowance (DAA), orSupplementary Disability Allowance (Asi).How to get the Puma?To make your application for entitlement, you must first complete a form:Application to open the rights to the Health InsurancePlease note Any person who deliberately refuses affiliate or who insists not to engage the steps for his compulsory affiliation to a social security scheme is punishable by imprisonment of 6 months and a fine of €15,000 (or only one of these penalties).Can the Puma be removed?Yes, the Puma can be withdrawn if you no longer meet the conditions of stability of residence or regularity of stay.Thus, for example, you must spontaneously declare your departure abroad. To do this, you complete this form.Declaration of transfer of residence outside FranceWho can help me?Find who can answer your questions in your region Search contact pointPivot Local Pivot Local What is your city or postal code ? rows.title: Best (and worst) areas and suburbs in Amsterdam | Expat Arrivals
rows.content: Skip to main content Main navigation Home Forum Guides Social Search User account menu Register Log in Breadcrumb Home Europe The Netherlands Amsterdam Areas and suburbs in Amsterdam MovingPros and Cons of MovingCost of LivingGetting AroundHealthcareWeatherWorkingAccommodationAreas and SuburbsSchoolsInternational SchoolsLifestyleCountry infoSchoolsAccommodationPros and Cons of MovingMoney and TaxesHealthcareLocal CultureCost of LivingDoing BusinessExpat Articles Download our Moving to Amsterdam Guide (PDF) The best places to live in AmsterdamLiving in Amsterdam offers a unique blend of old-world charm and modern innovation, perfectly suited to globally mobile, business-minded expats. This city provides an ideal environment for professionals seeking a balance between work and lifestyle.Here are some of the top areas and suburbs in Amsterdam offering prime expat-friendly accommodation, with amenities like international schools, cultural attractions, and excellent transport links making them ideal for expats.Read more about Utilities and Renting Accommodation in Amsterdam.Family-friendly areas of AmsterdamAmsterdam Oud-WestOud-West offers you the best of both worlds – the leisure perks of the city centre paired with touches of nature. From trendy cafés and museums to lively shopping streets like the Overtoom, you’ll always find something to do. And don’t forget Vondelpark, a favourite spot for locals and visitors alike.Residents in Oud-West include students, professionals, and expats, enjoying larger houses and even hidden gardens that add a touch of serenity to the area.Amsterdam-ZuidIn Amsterdam-Zuid, you’ll find a blend of peaceful living and premium amenities. This upscale area is perfect for families, offering playgrounds, parks, and exceptional schools, including the British School of Amsterdam. With landmarks like the Rijksmuseum and the Stedelijk Museum, as well as high-end shopping, there’s no shortage of ways to spend your time.Zuid’s well-maintained infrastructure and proximity to Vondelpark make it a top choice for families looking for a balanced lifestyle.WatergraafsmeerWatergraafsmeer stands out as one of Amsterdam’s greenest residential areas. Whether you’re relaxing in your garden or enjoying a stroll through local parks like Frankendael Park, this neighbourhood is all about outdoor living. It’s also home to the Jaap Edenbaan ice-skating rink, making it perfect for active families.The area offers a quiet, cosmopolitan vibe with reputable schools and a variety of good restaurants and bars to discover, making it ideal for families seeking suburban peace with city accessibility.WesterparkIf you’re raising a family, Westerpark is an excellent choice. This neighbourhood combines good schools with cultural attractions like the Westergasfabriek, a vibrant cultural hub hosting events and family-friendly activities. Designer boutiques, cafés, and a lively nightlife scene ensure there’s always something happening here.Westerpark is known for its community markets and festivals and expansive green spaces with ponds and playgrounds, adding to its charm for both residents and visitors.IJburgIJburg, a modern artificial archipelago in eastern Amsterdam, is ideal for families seeking waterfront living with a suburban feel. This area features contemporary architecture, spacious homes, and many outdoor spaces like beaches and parks. With new tram connections improving access to the city centre, IJburg is a rising star in Amsterdam’s housing market.You’ll find a laid-back vibe here, complemented by focusing on sustainable living and amenities designed for families.AmstelveenLocated just south of Amsterdam, Amstelveen is a haven for families seeking a quieter lifestyle. This leafy suburb offers spacious homes, excellent international schools, and family-friendly amenities like parks and playgrounds. The proximity to Amsterdam makes it a popular choice for expats who want suburban tranquillity without sacrificing urban convenience.HouthavensHouthavens is a former timber port, now transformed into a sustainable residential area. With eco-friendly homes and abundant green spaces, it’s perfect for families who value environmentally conscious living. The area also features modern amenities, playgrounds, and access to cultural attractions, offering a harmonious blend of urban life and nature.Areas for young and single expats in AmsterdamCentrumLiving in Centrum places you right in the heart of Amsterdam. This bustling area offers small but desirable apartments close to iconic attractions like the Anne Frank House and the Canal Belt. Whether strolling along Singel Canal or exploring De Wallen’s lively streets, you’ll experience the city’s dynamic energy.Centrum’s excellent connectivity makes it easy to get around, giving you more time to enjoy the world-class dining and cultural experiences on offer.Recent years have seen significant developments in Centrum’s housing market. Intense demand and limited supply have driven property prices up, with overbidding becoming common. This heightened competition makes securing premium apartments challenging, but the district remains a top choice for those drawn to its cultural richness and urban convenience.De BaarsjesLocated within the city’s central ring, De Baarsjes is perfect if you prefer a quieter pace of life while still being close to the action. Rembrandtpark offers a green escape, ideal for jogging or walking your dog, while the open-air market on Vespuccistraat brings a touch of local flavour to your doorstep.This neighbourhood’s affordability and low crime rate make it a popular choice for expats seeking balance and convenience. Known for its multicultural vibe, De Baarsjes offers trendy cafés and boutiques that cater to a youthful, energetic community.Indische BuurtIndische Buurt in eastern Amsterdam is a diverse neighbourhood with a rich expat history. Over half of the area’s residents are foreign-born, creating a cosmopolitan atmosphere where more than 100 languages are spoken. Accommodation here is mainly affordable apartments, offering you value without sacrificing access to the city’s amenities.With an influx of young professionals and students in recent years, Indische Buurt continues to evolve. Its street festivals, food markets, and art exhibitions reflect a lively cultural scene, making it a lively and inclusive place to live.Amsterdam-NoordAmsterdam-Noord, located across the IJ River, has transformed into an exciting cultural hub. Thanks to its creative spaces, trendy eateries, and cultural attractions, it's a favourite among young professionals and artists. The improved ferry services and proximity to the city centre make Noord an increasingly appealing option for those looking to experience Amsterdam’s dynamic energy while enjoying more space.The area’s recent growth includes new developments that blend modern living with historic charm, providing ample housing opportunities and cultural engagement. Areas to avoid in AmsterdamWhile Amsterdam is generally a safe city, there are a few areas where crime rates are higher or where noise and crowds may impact your experience. Understanding these nuances can help you make more informed decisions about where to live or visit.As the bustling heart of Amsterdam, Centrum experiences frequent pickpocketing and bicycle theft, particularly in crowded spots like Dam Square and surrounding attractions. Additionally, during peak tourist seasons, noise levels can rise significantly. While these factors may deter those seeking tranquillity, Centrum remains a top choice for expats drawn to its excellent connectivity, cultural richness, and vibrant urban lifestyle.Areas like the Red Light District, Museumplein, and Jordaan are magnets for visitors. During peak months from April to September, the influx of tourists can make these areas feel congested and less relaxing for residents. That said, Jordaan continues to attract expats seeking picturesque canals and boutique shops, blending charm with a lively atmosphere.Historically known for property crimes and vandalism, Bijlmermeer has undergone extensive urban renewal. While improvements are visible, some parts of the area still face challenges. Community policing and safety initiatives are actively addressing these issues.What areas of Amsterdam do expats love?"My favourite neighbourhoods are the Jordaan, the Pijp and Oud-Zuid, and of course, Watergraafsmeer. The Centre is beautiful and a great place to spend time outside – but I wouldn’t want to live there because it is crowded, too noisy and last but not least, quite expensive."Read our expat interview with Dana in Amsterdam for her take on the best areas for an expat to live."I think all of Amsterdam is fun. But the centre is very expensive and if you want to save on money try to pick the outskirts. Just be aware that the further out the less action you will see."Read Monique’s expat interview in Amsterdam, where she shares her unique experience."We are pretty happy in the centre of the city where we are now, although we do realise that this is not for everybody. Many of our expat friends and colleagues reside in Oud-Zuid, one of the more fashionable areas nowadays, or went to one of the surrounding cities like Almere."Edward gives some suggestions on popular neighbourhoods in this Amsterdam expat interview.Further reading►For more on finding the perfect home, see Accommodation in the NetherlandsPhoto credits: Amsterdam by Michal B; De Wallen by Zoltan Tasi. Find a Centre Find a Citizens Information Centre in your area: Carlow Cavan Clare Cork Donegal Dublin Galway Kerry Kildare Kilkenny Laois Leitrim Limerick Longford Louth Mayo Meath Monaghan Offaly Roscommon Sligo Tipperary Waterford Westmeath Wexford Wicklow Volunteering AskCI Categories What's New My Situation Find a Centre Volunteering AskCI You are here: Home > Money and Tax > Personal finance > Banking > Proof of identity to open a bank account Proof of identity to open a bank account Introduction Documents you can use to prove your identity How to apply Introduction When you open an account with a financial institution such as a bank or credit union, it must establish proof of your identity. This requirement is set down in anti-money laundering laws.The Central Bank has an explainer on why you must prove your identity when opening a bank account. Documents you can use to prove your identity When you are opening an account, you will need at least one form of photographic identification (photo ID) to prove your identity and at least one document to prove your address. You cannot use the same document as proof of both your identity and your address. Examples of documents that banks may accept as photo ID include:Valid passportValid driving licenceIrish Government Travel DocumentTemporary Residence CertificateIrish Residency PermitYour proof of identity must be in date. The name on your photo ID must match the name on your proof of address.Examples of documents that banks may accept as proof of your address include:Current utility bill (such as a gas, electricity or phone bill)Current car or home insurance policy that shows your addressDocument issued by a government department that shows your addressCopy of your Tax Credit Certificate (TCC)Statement of Liability from RevenueYour proof of address must be less than 6 months old (or 12 months for an insurance policy).In some cases a bank may ask you for your PPS number – for example, if you are claiming tax relief on the interest paid on a mortgage loan.Copies of the documents you use to establish your identity must be kept by the bank for 5 years after an account is closed.If you cannot provide the standard documentsIf you cannot provide the standard documents requested, contact the bank for advice on alternatives that may be acceptable.There is a guide to opening a bank account for refugees and asylum seekers (pdf). You can also download the guide for international protection applicants in other languages.Requests for information on transactionsBank staff must know the nature of their customers' business and can ask for information about the level and type of business that is likely to be transacted through the account. You can also be asked to provide confirmation of the source of your funds and to give reasons for carrying out certain transactions. How to apply Contact your bank or financial institution to get full details of the identification it requires. Read More > July 17, 2026 DHS Publishes Final Rule Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of Stay ProcedureRead More > July 6, 2026 Summer DSO Refresher: Managing Breaks in StudyRead More > See All Blogs > Blog Tools Go to Tools Page Popular Links School Search SEVIS Data Mapping Tool Guide to Studying in the States Resource Library School Certification Life Cycle Help Hubs Go to Help Hubs Popular Links SEVIS Help Hub SEVP Portal Help STEM OPT Hub SEVP Fraud Hub Filter Students Resources for Students Breadcrumb Home Students Obtaining a Social Security Number Obtaining a Social Security Number Last updated: May 25, 2023 The Social Security Administration (SSA) assigns nine-digit Social Security numbers (SSNs) to U.S. citizens, permanent residents and eligible nonimmigrant workers in the United States. SSA uses SSNs to report wages to the government, track Social Security benefits and for other identification purposes. Every F and M student who U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) grants employment authorization to needs an SSN. Please note: If an F or M student (or dependent) is ineligible to receive an SSN, but receives non-wage income while in the United States (e.g., scholarships, grants, interest on stocks, gambling/lottery winnings), they must apply for an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN). For more information, please visit our What is an ITIN? resource page. Steps for Obtaining a Social Security Number If you want to receive an SSN while studying in the United States, follow these steps: 1. Talk with your DSO about working and training in the United States. Your DSO will share important information regarding the regulations and requirements for F and M students, and confirm whether you are eligible to apply for an SSN. 2. Verify you are in Active status in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS). Your SEVIS record must be in Active status for at least two days before applying for an SSN. If you have a record in any other status, you will not be successful in applying for an SSN. 3. Wait 10 days after arriving in the United States before applying for an SSN to allow enough time for your arrival information to update in all government systems. SSA uses the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) program to verify your nonimmigrant student status and determine if you are eligible for an SSN. You can use the SAVE Case Check to follow the progress of your SAVE verification check online; visit our Checking Your SAVE Case Status for more information. 4. Visit your local SSA office. You can file your application for an SSN card in person at any SSA office. Be prepared to provide your original documents to prove your age, identity and work-authorized immigration status. All evidence of immigration status and work authorization must be unexpired. For more information on the types of documents you need to apply for an SSN, refer to the SSA website. Social Security Numbers and Driver’s Licenses Many states require that you or your dependent have an SSN or have already applied for one before you apply for a driver's license. In these states, if you or your dependents are not eligible to work but want to apply for a driver's license, you must first apply for an SSN at the local SSA office and receive a Form SSA-L676, "Refusal to Process SSN Application." To learn more, visit our Driving in the States page and talk with your DSO.
