Definition and application processWhat is the Beckham Law?How does taxation of foreigners in Spain work without the Beckham’s Law?How does taxation of foreigners in Spain work after the Beckham’s law?Tax on Spanish Income vs Worldwide IncomeWho can apply for the Beckham Law regime?Who cannot apply for Beckham’s law?Beckham Law in Spain: RequirementsTax reductions under the Beckham LawCapital Gains TaxInheritance TaxProperty TaxWhat are the benefits of Beckham’s law for expats?DisadvantagesHow to apply for the Beckham Law in Spain?Application deadlines to the Beckham tax regimeTax advice on the Beckham’s Law from LawantsRelated articlesWhat is the Beckham Rule in Spain? Definition and application processThe Beckham Law in Spain represents a significant fiscal opportunity for expatriates working within its borders. Initially established to attract top talent and investment, this regulation offers a substantial tax reduction on Spanish taxable income for eligible individuals. In the intricate landscape of Spanish taxation, where general tax rates can soar as high as 54% in Valencia, 47% in Catalonia, and 45% in Madrid, the Beckham Law can cap tax liabilities at a more palatable 24% for incomes up to €600,000. This article delves into the intricacies of the Beckham Rule, outlining its purpose, application criteria, and the process for claiming its benefits. For entrepreneurs and professionals considering Spain as a business hub, understanding and leveraging the Beckham Law can be pivotal in maximizing investment returns and minimizing fiscal burdens.What is the Beckham Law?The Beckham Law, officially known as the Special Expats’ Tax Regime (SETR), is a Spanish fiscal policy tailored to attract international talent and qualified workers to Spain.Enacted through Royal Decree 687/2005 and integrated within the Spanish Income Tax Act, this law offers a preferential tax treatment to expatriates, allowing them to be taxed at a flat rate of 24% on their Spanish-sourced income rather than the standard progressive tax rates applicable to worldwide income, which can range from 19% to 45%.This advantageous tax regime applies during the first six years of residency in Spain, providing substantial savings and making Spain an attractive destination for global professionals.Historically, the Beckham Law garnered its moniker from the English football icon David Beckham, who was among the first to benefit from this decree upon joining Real Madrid. The law’s primary goal was to bolster Spain’s appeal as a hub for exceptional talent by easing the tax load for affluent foreign workers. While originally inclusive of sports professionals, amendments have since excluded this group.As of January 1st, 2023, further modifications have expanded eligibility to a broader range of expatriates, including those employed by foreign companies—a move aimed at stimulating Spain’s burgeoning start-up ecosystem.Under this regime, not only the applicant but also their spouse and children under 25 are entitled to preferential tax treatment on their income and assets located within Spain. However, it’s essential to note that despite these benefits, capital gains and investment incomes sourced in Spain are still subject to taxation at rates between 19% and 28%.In essence, the Beckham Law offers a strategic fiscal advantage for high-earning expatriates relocating to Spain by redefining tax residency and reducing the complexity and burden of tax liabilities on their income generated within Spanish territory.Benefit from Beckham’s Law with Lawant’s expert tax consultancy. Whether you’re an expatriate or employing foreign professionals, our specialists provide clear, strategic guidance to optimize your tax benefits under this regime. Contact us and don’t miss out on the opportunity to enhance your financial efficiency in Spain. Tax ConsultancyA tax consultancy is in charge of financial counseling and advising clients about any update or tax requirements. It advice according on how […]Read More… from Tax Consultancy Find out moreHow does taxation of foreigners in Spain work without the Beckham’s Law?Prior to the introduction of the Beckham Law in 2005, foreign nationals residing in Spain were fully integrated into the standard Spanish tax system. Upon spending more than six months (183 days) within a calendar year in Spain, they would be classified as tax residents. This status brought with it the obligation to pay taxes on their worldwide income under the Impuesto sobre la Renta de las Personas Físicas (IRPF), or Personal Income Tax.Under this traditional regime, expatriates were subject to the same progressive tax rates as Spanish citizens, which could escalate up to 54% depending on their income level. The tax system was structured such that the percentage of tax owed increased progressively with income—starting at 19% for lower income brackets and rising for those earning above €60,000.This meant that foreign residents not only had to declare and pay taxes on their income earned within Spain but also on any income generated abroad.The implementation of the Beckham Law dramatically altered this scenario for qualifying individuals by introducing a fixed reduced tax rate and limiting the taxable base to Spanish-sourced income for a set period, thus offering a significant financial incentive for high-earning professionals considering a move to Spain.This special regime is particularly advantageous for those earning more than €60,000.Read also our guide to buying a house in Spain.How does taxation of foreigners in Spain work after the Beckham’s law?The advent of the Beckham Law revolutionized the tax landscape for expatriates in Spain. Under this regime, the rigid boundaries of tax residency were redefined, allowing qualifying foreign workers to benefit from a more favorable tax treatment, similar to that of non-residents, during the first year they become residents and the following five years, depending on when they arrive in the country.The primary alteration brought about by the Beckham Law is that even if expatriates spend over 183 days in Spain and are considered tax residents, they are taxed under a special set of rules. Specifically, they are only required to pay Spanish income tax on the income earned within Spain. Instead of being subject to the standard progressive tax rates, which increase with income levels, individuals under the Beckham Law are liable for a flat rate of 24% on earnings up to €600,000. For any income exceeding this threshold, a fixed rate of 45% is applied.This special taxation method offers a substantial financial advantage as it significantly lowers the potential tax rate compared to the standard resident rates that can peak at 45%. The savings are particularly pronounced for high-earning expatriates who, without this law, would face a much steeper tax obligation. By capping the tax rate at a lower fixed percentage, the Beckham Law provides an attractive fiscal incentive for expatriates and has become a pivotal consideration for those looking to optimize their tax position while working in Spain.Tax on Spanish Income vs Worldwide IncomeOne of the most salient features of the Beckham Law is its focus on taxation of Spanish-sourced income, to the exclusion of worldwide income. Under this regime, expatriates are required to pay taxes only on the income that is generated within Spanish territory. This starkly contrasts with the obligations of tax residents who must report and pay taxes on their global income, making the Beckham Law particularly advantageous for those with diverse international income streams.This targeted approach allows expatriates to structure their finances in a manner that minimizes their tax liability in Spain while simultaneously reducing risk through income diversification. The wealth tax, for instance, does not apply to assets located abroad, but it taxes wealth, not income such as dividends. Income tax taxes income, like dividends.However, there is an important caveat: employment income earned abroad remains taxable under normal rates. Even though expatriates are considered non-residents for tax purposes under the Beckham Law, they are still obliged to pay Spanish tax on foreign employment income. Nevertheless, Spain’s tax system offers mechanisms to prevent double taxation; taxes paid abroad can often be credited against Spanish tax liabilities under certain conditions.For expatriates earning above a certain threshold, it’s crucial to evaluate whether the Beckham Law is financially beneficial. Low-income earners might find the progressive tax rates more favorable, especially if their earnings fall below regional thresholds where progressive rates could be as low as 0%.It’s also important to note that those opting for the Beckham Law may not qualify for other Spanish tax benefits such as home rental income relief or deductions related to disabilities and dependents. Additionally, because the Beckham Law positions expatriates as non-residents for tax purposes, they cannot take advantage of Spain’s double taxation treaties that would normally prevent being taxed twice on the same income—a significant consideration for those with international financial dealings.Who can apply for the Beckham Law regime?While the Beckham Law in Spain opens the door to tax advantages for many is designed to benefit a diverse group of foreign individuals who choose to relocate to Spain. Eligibility for application to the spanish Beckham Rule regime extends to:Foreign workers who relocate to Spain to engage in an economic activity, specifically those employed by a company.Expatriates who hold managerial positions or other significant roles are considered among the administrators or employees, as the law does not specify this as a separate category.Individuals who move to Spain with the intention of performing remote work for an employer.Highly qualified professionals who offer services to start-up companies, or are involved in training, research, development, and innovation (R&D&I) activities, with at least 40% of their income derived from invoicing related to these services.Company administrators who take up positions in Spain, provided they do not own more than 25% of a company that is classified as asset-managing. Importantly, administrators can have more than a 25% ownership stake if the company is not considered an asset-management entity. In these cases, we recommend creating a wholly-owned LLC (SL) that engages in economic activity.Family members of the remote workers, which includes the spouse and any dependents.Who cannot apply for Beckham’s law?While the Beckham Law in Spain opens the door to tax advantages for many expatriates, there are specific exclusions to be aware of. The following groups are not eligible to apply for the Beckham’s Law regime:Freelancers or self-employed individuals, including those possessing a digital nomad visa.Sports professionals, including athletes, irrespective of their income level or status within their respective fields.It is incorrect to state that directors with ownership stakes exceeding 25% in Spanish companies are excluded. They are eligible, provided their company is not classified as asset-managing or if they apply under a startup or entrepreneur visa.Beckham Law in Spain: RequirementsTo harness the fiscal benefits of the spanish Beckham Law, expatriates must meet a specific set of requirements. It is crucial for individuals to assess their eligibility before proceeding with the application. If you are considering applying for the Beckham Law, here are the essential criteria you need to satisfy:The applicant must not have been a tax resident in Spain during the five years prior to their relocation for employment purposes.They must be relocating to Spain for work, with an employment offer, a digital nomad visa, a transfer from a foreign company, or be a director with ownership exceeding 25% in a company that is not classified as asset-managing (unless possessing a startup/entrepreneur visa).The work performed in Spain should be the primary source of the applicant’s professional activity. This means that any income classified as obtained through a permanent establishment must come from highly qualified economic activity or entrepreneurial activity. The employer can be a Spanish or foreign corporate entity, but the income should not be attributed to a permanent establishment in Spain.The employer can be a Spanish or foreign corporate entity, but income should not be attributed to a permanent establishment in Spain.The deadline for applying to the regime is six months from either the registration with Social Security or arrival in Spain, whichever comes first.It is imperative to note that these conditions extend to the applicant’s spouse and dependent children under 25, as well as elderly parents or disabled individuals who relocate with the taxpayer within the first fiscal year for which the regime is applicable. We strongly recommend contacting our team to verify if you meet all the requirements for applying for Beckham’s Law and to guide you through the application process. Tax ConsultancyA tax consultancy is in charge of financial counseling and advising clients about any update or tax requirements. It advice according on how […]Read More… from Tax Consultancy Find out moreTax reductions under the Beckham LawThe Beckham Law is not only a game-changer for income tax but also offers a broader spectrum of tax advantages. By allowing expatriates to be taxed as non-resident taxpayers on their Spanish-sourced income, the Beckham Law presents a fixed flat rate, alleviating the tax load for high earners who would otherwise face steep progressive tax rates. The impact of the Beckham Rule extends beyond income tax; it provides an optimized tax structure across various fiscal obligations in Spain. Under this regime, expatriates are only taxed on income generated within Spanish territory, thereby excluding foreign-sourced wealth such as rental income, dividends, interest, and capital gains accrued outside of Spain from the Spanish tax net.All employment income is taxed at 24/47%, and any withholding tax can be recovered through deduction to avoid double taxation, mechanisms are in place to prevent double taxation, allowing expatriates to offset taxes paid elsewhere against their Spanish tax liabilities.However, it’s essential for expatriates to evaluate whether the Beckham Law aligns with their financial situation. For those with lower incomes, the progressive tax rates—which can dip as low as 0%—may prove more beneficial. The decision to opt for the Beckham Law should be made after careful consideration of individual earnings and potential eligibility for other tax benefits that may not be available under this special regime.Capital Gains TaxUnder the Beckham Law, capital gains tax is subject to specific conditions that differ from the standard Spanish tax system. While the Beckham Law does not exempt capital gains, it does offer a structured tax rate for expatriates. Dividends and profits derived from the sale of both movable and immovable properties within Spain are taxed at a variable rate, which is determined by the gain amount and ranges from 19% to 28%.It is crucial for expatriates to recognize that while the Beckham Law provides relief on capital gains generated in Spain, it does not extend to those realized outside of Spanish territory. Capital gains accrued abroad remain subject to taxation in the respective countries according to their local laws. Expatriates must ensure compliance with international tax obligations, as income obtained outside of Spain does not escape taxation simply because it is not taxable under the Spanish Beckham regime.Inheritance TaxThe Beckham Law regime has no impact on inheritance and gift tax, as it does not change the general regime of this tax is tailored to resemble that of non-residents, despite the individual’s de facto resident status. This alignment means that under the Beckham Law, expatriates are subject to the same inheritance and gift tax rules as those who are not permanent residents of Spain. The application of non-resident tax rates to inheritance and donations provides a significant tax reduction for beneficiaries and donors under the Beckham regime, effectively extending the financial benefits of this special tax status beyond income tax to encompass pivotal life events involving asset transfers.Property TaxThe Beckham Law provides a strategic tax advantage for expatriates concerning Property tax, or IBI, taxes only properties in Spain, while the wealth tax only applies to assets in Spain and can be managed through an investment strategy outside the country. Specifically, under this special regime, property tax is levied solely on real estate assets located within Spain. This targeted approach ensures that expatriates benefiting from the Beckham Law are not burdened by wealth tax on their assets located outside Spain, significantly reducing their overall tax liability. For instance, an expatriate with a portfolio valued at 3 million euros would be subject to a wealth tax of approximately 1.79% on their Spanish properties alone. This focused taxation under the Beckham Law offers a substantial financial incentive for foreign investors and workers considering property acquisition in Spain as part of their wealth management strategy.What are the benefits of Beckham’s law for expats?Expatriates in Spain can enjoy numerous benefits under the Beckham law, which include:A reduced flat tax rate of 24% on income up to €600,000, compared to the progressive rates of up to 54% for residents (in Valencia).Taxation on Spanish-sourced income only, rather than worldwide income, which can lead to significant tax savings.Wealth tax obligations are limited to Spanish assets, excluding global wealth from the taxable base.No obligation to file the Modelo 720, a declaration of overseas assets, which simplifies tax compliance and prese

rows.content: Facebook Twitter Instagram Linkedin Youtube +34 936 31 51 39 Home Services Immigration Services Get your Residence Permit Digital Nomad Visa Highly Qualified Professional Non-Lucrative Visa Work Permit Entrepreneur Visa Family Member of an EU Citizen Student Visa Arraigo All immigration lawyer sevices Business Legal Advice Register as a freelance Set up a company All business laywer services Tax Optimization & Accounting Beckham Law Accounting Taxes in Spain for Expats: For Residents and Non-Residents All tax lawyer services Real Estate Buy a property in Spain All property lawyer services Legal Services Legal Advice for Expats in Spain Make a will Inheritance law Civil Partnership Debt Recovery All civil lawyer services Book appointment Blog Spanish Property News Tax News in Spain Legal: Civil, Family and Labour Law in Spain Immigration in Spain News Business Legal News in Spain View all articles About Contact Book appointment Select Page Home » Real Estate » Renting a property in Spain: complete guide for expats Renting a property in Spain: complete guide for expats by Balcells Group International Lawyers | Real Estate Are you considering renting in Spain? Then in this complete guide you will find everything you need to know. We will navigate through the most important issues to consider. From market conditions to apartment prices, where to find a flat and which are the legal clauses and requirements you will need to meet. Including some really useful tips at the end that have helped tons of expats in Spain! Content hide 1 How does renting a property in Spain work? 1.1 Most typical rental conditions 1.2 Types of rental contracts 2 Steps to renting a property in Spain 2.1 1. Find a property to rent 2.2 2. Check the state of the property 2.3 3. Sign the rental contract 2.4 4. Moving in and utilities 3 Documents and requirements to rent a property in Spain as expat 3.1 Entry deposits 3.2 Legal requirements 4 Best areas to rent a property 5 Rental prices 6 Cost of monthly bills 7 Extra tips for an easy rental in Spain 8 FAQs about renting a property in Spain 8.1 How long does it take to sign a rental agreement? 8.2 Is it possible to negotiate the rent price in Spain? 8.3 How do I overcome language barrier when renting a property? 8.4 What are the exiting conditions of a rental? 9 Should you buy or should you rent? How does renting a property in Spain work? Let’s start by providing a general overview of the Spanish rental market that will help you understand later sections. First of all, we are talking about a market that is not quite advanced and whose main characteristic is a lack of trust. Traditionally tenants have gained the fame of being bad payers. Being because they usually pay late (or not pay at all), landlords have become more and more skeptic and in search of legal protection. This, for sure, has affected the market. But how? First of all, nowadays the vast majority of landlords reach out to real estate agencies to act as intermediaries. This ensures that they get paid at the end of each month, as they are not the ones directly in contact with the tenant. Of course, and as we will see below, this affects the total price the renter has to pay. On the other hand, this reluctancy to trust the roomer has made that many properties that were the result of real estate investments have become completely empty and nearly forgotten. With the aim to avoid legal conflict, many owners decided not to rent. This puts pressure on prices, as usually the demand is not matched with enough offer. Most typical rental conditions And what about the conditions of the typical rental? What you need to know is that in Spain what you rent the vast majority of the time is a flat (or apartment), and not a big house. Sizes differ from 1 to 3 bedrooms, but during the past years, the size of the flats rented has been going down. The result? The average flat size is 90 square meters with 2 bedrooms. And for 1 bedroom apartments (which are also typical), size can go down until 50-60 square meters. We are mentioning this last point as it is really common in Spain to just rent one room inside a shared flat. It’s the case of foreign citizens who come to the country for their Erasmus or masters; or for individuals in search of a job. Types of rental contracts Finally, you should be aware that there are two types of contracts: First of all, we find the short-term contracts (called “contrato de arrendamiento de temporada” in Spanish), which go from 6 months (minimum) until 1 year (maximum). Those have lower legal protections. And on the other hand, we find long-term contracts (“arriendo de vivienda”), which last for longer than a year. I want to speak to a lawyer Steps to renting a property in Spain In the next section, you will find an overview of the main steps you must take in order to successfully rent a property in the Spanish territory. Including useful tips for expats! 1. Find a property to rent Let’s now move to the first step of the process: finding a flat to rent. In general, you have three different options. The first one is to walk down the street in those areas that you most enjoy our would like living, and search for rental property billboards announcing that the flat is for rent. They are usually red or orange, and have the words “se alquila” plusa phone number to contact. If you are interested in that particular flat, you just need to call that number and ask for additional information. The second alternative is going to a real estate agency. They have tons of properties listed, so finding the right option for you is somewhat easy. The problem is that they will charge you a commission, being as an extra rental month payment once you enter into the flat, or as an extra percentage of your rent each month. Hence, our advice is that you avoid agencies and go to directly talk to the landlord/property owner. It will save you money! Finally, the third option is searching online in any of the portals out there. The main ones are: Idealista Fotocasa Servihabitat Searching inside those will enable you to cover nearly 95% of all listings in the area, so those are more than enough. Nevertheless, bear in mind that during the past years, real estate agencies have also been moving to those platforms, so finding a landlord inside them is more tricky nowadays. 2. Check the state of the property Once you have found what seems like THE property, make sure to check its state, in depth. That is essential before putting down a deposit or paying any type of fee. Here you must validate and consider things like: The person you are trying to sign a rental agreement with is the real and actual property owner In case the place was a commercial property before, it has what’s called “cedula de habitabilidad” The conditions of the flat/house are ok In case you cannot visit the property in person, make sure to request a video or to have someone visit for you. 3. Sign the rental contract The next step would be to sign the rental contract with the property owner directly, or with the real estate agency in case there is one. Of course, checking each and every single clause will be crucial. Make sure to check: That the monthly price is the one you agreed with If the owner has the right to increase the price, and when The exit conditions Who will pay for taxes such as IBI or other municipality taxes When will you recover the deposit Bear in mind that at this point you will have to make a down payment, which can be equal to 1 or 2 months of rent. 4. Moving in and utilities Finally, once the rental contract is signed, you will be able to move to the property and bring all your belongings. Of course, here you will face one of the most tedious parts of the process, which is changing the name of the different utilities and services such as water, electricity, and gas. Usually, this means that the first consumption will be paid by the last invoice paid by the landlord before the change of name comes into effect. Documents and requirements to rent a property in Spain as expat What documents will you have to prepare when renting a house or flat in the Spanish territory? Entry deposits When renting a property in Spain, landlords typically require tenants to pay an initial deposit and, in some cases, additional upfront fees. Here’s what to expect: Security deposit (fianza). By law, landlords can request a minimum of one month’s rent as a deposit for unfurnished properties and two months for furnished properties. This deposit is held in a government-regulated entity and is refundable upon lease termination if no damages occur. First month’s tent. In most cases, landlords require the first month’s rent upfront before handing over the keys. Agency fees. If a real estate agency is involved, expect to pay an additional fee equivalent to one month’s rent(some regions, like Catalonia, prohibit landlords from passing agency fees to tenants). Additional guarantees. Landlords may request an extra financial guarantee (aval bancario) equivalent to three to six months of rent, especially if the tenant lacks a stable income source in Spain. Legal requirements To secure a rental agreement, expats must provide certain documents to verify their identity and financial stability. These typically include: Valid passport or NIE, which are required for contract signing and legal identification. Proof of income. Landlords often require: Spanish employment contract & recent pay slips (“nóminas”), if employed Proof of self-employment income or tax returns, if self-employed A bank statement showing sufficient savings (if unemployed or retired) Employment reference or guarantor.Some landlords can request a letter from your employer or a guarantor (avalista) if your income source is outside Spain Bank account in Spain. Rent is typically paid via bank transfer, so opening a Spanish bank account is advisable Best areas to rent a property Once you start looking for apartments you will start asking yourself which is the best area to do so. You will find pretty good offers, but perhaps you are not 100% convinced about its location. Which is the rule to follow here? As always, it depends. Obviously, the closest to the city center, the more action, and dynamism. But the higher the prices. What we can suggest is that you carefully look for locations that have good public transport connections. In big cities like Madrid or Barcelona, having a metro station nearby is crucial, as those lines work fast and perfectly well. So having a metro stop in front of your door is of great value. Also, having a big supermarket close by is perhaps another important checkmark. In the end, you will be going there every now and then, so it can avoid tedious movements. Nevertheless, something you can also do that will be highly beneficial is to ask others that were in the same situation before. If you go to Facebook, there are tons of expat groups in any of the Spanish cities. Search for your local group, join, and ask its members for their recommendations. That will provide really useful insights! Rental prices This is for sure one of the most important things to consider: how much should you pay to rent a flat in the Spanish territory? The bad news is that there is no fixed answer. Rental prices vary drastically according to many factors. Those factors are the city in which you are renting, the location inside that city (the closer to the city center, the more you’ll pay), if the flat is interior or exterior (it has windows facing the street or not), if it has public transport connections nearby, the flat size, etc. Besides, the real estate market is unpredictable, prices can vary widely from one year to another. Nevertheless, as we are sure that you need at least a vague reference, here are the numbers: Renting a single room in a shared flat can cost you between 200 to 600€ per month (being the expensive extreme not really common even though we are talking about big cities). Studios or flats for two individuals can cost from 500 to1000€ per month. Here’s an overview of how much you can expect to pay, per month, in each of the most popular Spanish cities: City Average Rent (1-Bedroom Apartment in City Center) Average Rent (3-Bedroom Apartment in City Center) Estimated Monthly Living Costs (Single Person, Excluding Rent) Barcelona €1,290.97 €2,197.33 €817 Madrid €1,034.15 €1,900 €794 Valencia €958.61 €1,501.39 €1,581 Seville €1,243 €1,358 €1,358 Zaragoza €724 €1,330 €1,330 Málaga €1,062 €1,519 €1,519 Bilbao €1,243 €1,522 €1,522 Alicante €700 €1,200 €1,200 Córdoba €650 €1,100 €1,100 Granada €600 €1,000 €1,000 Usually, flats are comprehensive and already have a washing machine and fridge, so you won’t need to pay that extra. They are usually also fully furnished, with a complete kitchen and utensils. Finally, the good news is that there is always room for negotiation. If you directly go to a landlord, it is possible to negotiate and get a reduced price than what you saw online. Cost of monthly bills Even though there’s a fixed monthly price you need to pay as a rental, that’s not the whole story. Apart from that, is it highly possible that you will need to pay extra. So the first thing to consider here is your contract, as paying extra or not will hugely depend on that. There are some rentals that with the fixed monthly price you get everything included: light, gas, water, wifi, etc. Nevertheless, other times those utilities must be paid separately. It can be that just water is included, or just electricity, or both but you still need to pay for the internet, etc. Each contract is a different world. That is why you should take that into consideration, carefully read the contract, and negotiate with the landlord. In case you are sharing a flat, the usual thing is to divide the total cost of the monthly utility bills into each tenant. Nevertheless, that is something that shouldn’t scare you. In Spain, utilities are not expensive. Water services are cheap, and finding a bundled package that includes both house internet and sim card is also possible. So in case your contract did not include ANY kind of utility, you could expect to pay, maximum (and for the whole thing), from 50 to 150€ per month. Then, there is also a special type of extra cost that could exist: community expenses. Suppose that the flat where you live has a common swimming pool are any other shared space like a garden or park. Usually, those areas have maintenance costs, which have to be paid by the whole neighbor community every single month. It is possible that your rental price already includes that cost, or that you need to pay it apart. Finally, you can also expect to pay small reparations like any water damage, in case your contract does not contemplate that. Let us help you! Extra tips for an easy rental in Spain Let’s now dive into some of the tips that will help you rent in Spain while avoiding legal problems: First of all, make sure to avoid verbal tenancy contracts. Always go for the written option. Carefully read the contract, and never sign without reading it. Even though the tenant is putting pressure on you as time is kicking, you always need to give it a profound read as to find any clause that goes against your interests. Don’t sign anything and don’t send out any kind of payment without visiting the flat before. In Spain, everything is done face to face, so if you want to avoid scams, go and visit the apartment. Try to avoid foreign country real estate listings (those that are not from Spain) when trying to find a flat, as they tend to be much more expensive. On the first day you enter the flat, take pictures of everything. Try to get the current status of each and every room, detecting any imperfection, note down if something like the light is not working properly, etc. Register each item and its state. This initial tracking will be crucial to avoid losing part of your deposit when leaving. Be quick and ready to give a fast response. In Spain, things move fast. It is possible that on the first day you visit the falt, the landlord asks for the deposit. So make sure to get it ready beforehand, or at least to be ready to provide a response stating if you like the apartment or not. Don’t be late with your payments. If you haven’t paid your rent after the 7th of any month, the house owner can legally request the money against at court. The process is really agile, if the amount to be paid is less than 2.000€, they can claim the money without a lawyer, obtaining a resolution in just two weeks. So make sure to pay when you should. FAQs about renting a property in Spain How long does it take to sign a rental agreement? The process of signing a rental agreement in Spain can take anywhere from a few days to two weeks, depending on factors such as document verification, deposit payments, and landlord approval. If you have all the required paperwork seen above (passport/NIE, proof of income, deposit, and first month’s rent) ready, you can finalize the contract within 48–72 hours. However, if negotiations or additional checks are needed, it may take longer. The part of the process that typically takes longer is the one concerning finding a property, which can be quite tedious nowadays in big cities like Madrid or Barcelona. Is it possible to negotiate the rent price in Spain? Yes, negotiating the rental price is common and often expected, especially in slower rental markets or if the property has been listed for a long time. Nevertheless, in cities like Madrid or Barcelona where the demand is much greater than the offer of flats, there is not much room for negotiation. Nevertheless, in smaller cities, landlords are often more flexible. If that is the case, factors that can help in negotiations include: Offering to pay several months upfront Signing a longer lease agreement Committing to handling minor repairs instead of the landlord Researching similar properties to justify your offer How do I overcome language barrier when renting a property? Many landlords and agencies speak basic English, especially in major cities, but rental contracts and negotiations are typically conducted in Spanish. Here’s how to navigate the language barrier: Use a bilingual real estate agent who specializes in helping expats Request a contract translation before signing Hire a relocation consultant or lawyer to review documents Use translation apps for day-to-day communication with landlords Being prepared with basic Spanish rental terms can also help—terms like “fianza” (deposit) and “contrato de alquiler” (rental contract) are useful to know. What are the exiting conditions of a rental? It is also worth mentioning the exit conditions. You must notify the landlord that you are planning to leave, and you must do so minimum 30 days before. You have the right of doing that in case you haven’t signed a contract that forces you to stay longer. In that case, you will need to pay for the difference, even though you are not living there anymore. For example, suppose that you agreed to rent for 12 months. On month number 8, you decide to leave. Therefore, you still need to pay the 4 remaining months. Once you deliver the house keys back, you will be allowed to receive the deposit back. What we recommend is that you request a house inspection of all the rooms, furniture, and any other element that could be damaged. As you made an initial inventory with everything in the house and took pictures of the current state of the apartment when entering (something you really should do), you will be able to compare with the inspection results. Once that is done, the landlord will pay the deposit back, even though she legally has 30 days of delay available. Should you buy or should you rent? Another common question. And, even though there is no right answer, there is the “safest” option. Our suggestion is simple: start renting out. See if the city fits what you were looking for, and once you fully decide y

rows.title: The 7 Biggest Mistakes When Moving to Spain
rows.content: Skip to content Home Services Contact Book a Consultation Home Services Contact Book a Consultation Menu The 7 Biggest Mistakes When Moving to Spain Written byFrancisco Ordeig FournierLawyer · Bar registration number 2330Last updated: May 12, 2026Moving to Spain offers an incredible lifestyle, from sun-drenched coastlines to bustling city centres. However, that dream can quickly sour if you fall into common administrative traps. In our experience as a nationwide Spanish legal and tax firm, we see the same preventable issues derail relocation plans time and again. These aren’t minor inconveniences; they are significant errors that can lead to visa rejections, unexpected tax bills, and months of bureaucratic limbo. This article outlines the 7 biggest mistakes when moving to spain and provides clear, practical steps to avoid them. We’ll skip the generic advice and focus on the technical details that truly matter. You’ll learn why choosing the correct visa from the start is non-negotiable, how to correctly establish your tax residency to avoid penalties, and what you must do to set up your business or freelance status properly. Before you even consider moving, understanding the administrative requirements and navigating the notarization process for various documents can save you significant time and stress. This guide is for professionals, entrepreneurs, and families who need to get their relocation right the first time. We’ll cover the specific challenges related to visas, taxes, business registration, healthcare, and rental contracts. By understanding these pitfalls, you can ensure your move is smooth and compliant, letting you focus on enjoying your new life in Spain. Let’s get started. 1. Underestimating the NIE and Tax Residency One of the most common and damaging mistakes we see is underestimating the importance of your NIE (Número de Identidad de Extranjero) and tax residency. Many new arrivals treat these as secondary tasks, only to discover they are foundational to almost every aspect of life here. Without a NIE, you can’t sign a rental contract, open a bank account, set up utilities, or even buy a car. It’s the administrative key that unlocks your new life in Spain. Similarly, your tax residency status determines where and how you pay taxes. This isn’t something you simply declare; it’s determined by specific rules. You become a tax resident if you spend more than 183 days in Spain during a calendar year or if your main center of economic or vital interests is here. Ignoring this can lead to serious financial consequences, including penalties for non-compliance and unexpected tax bills on your worldwide income. Real-World Consequences The problems caused by these delays aren’t theoretical. In our experience, they create immediate, stressful roadblocks. A digital nomad arrives ready to work but can’t register as self-employed (autónomo) or invoice clients because they delayed their NIE appointment. This halts their income and puts them in a difficult position with Spain’s tax agency, the Agencia Tributaria. An expat couple relocates for a job. They assume only the working spouse is a tax resident. Without proper advice, they’re shocked to learn both may be considered tax residents based on the “center of vital interests” rule, exposing their global assets to Spanish taxation. Delays in securing your NIE or clarifying tax residency create a domino effect. A simple administrative step, when missed, can halt your ability to work, rent, and comply with the law, costing you time and money. How to Get It Right from the Start You can avoid these issues with proactive planning. The key is to address your NIE and tax status before or immediately upon arrival. Secure Your NIE: Book your appointment online via the Sede Electrónica for the Policía Nacional before you even travel. You can often do this through a Spanish consulate in your home country. Gather Your Documents: For your NIE appointment, you’ll need the completed EX-15 form, your passport and a copy, proof of why you need the NIE (like a job offer), and proof of payment of the fee (Modelo 790-012). Define Your Tax Status: If you spend over 183 days in Spain, you are a tax resident. It’s that simple. Understanding this from day one allows you to plan effectively and explore beneficial regimes like the Beckham Law. For a detailed breakdown of your obligations, you can learn more about taxes for expats in Spain. We specialize in securing NIEs online across Spain and providing clear guidance on tax residency to ensure your move is smooth from the very beginning. Contact us for personalized advice. Need Legal Guidance?Need help with your case in Spain?If this article applies to your situation, contact our team for tailored legal guidance and clear next steps.Contact UsBook a Consultation2. Choosing the Wrong Visa for Your Circumstances Selecting an inappropriate visa is a fundamental error that can completely derail your plans to move to Spain. We see this often: people underestimate the strictness of visa categories or try to work around the system, leading to legal complications, residency denials, and even forced departure. Each visa—be it the Digital Nomad, Non-Lucrative, or Work visa—has precise requirements for income, employment status, and activity that are not interchangeable. The Spanish immigration authorities (Extranjería) are very clear: your visa must align with your actual economic activity. Attempting to enter Spain on a tourist visa to work remotely, for example, is a direct violation that can result in fines, deportation, and a ban on re-entry. The visa you choose isn’t just an entry permit; it defines your legal and financial rights and obligations in the country, from your ability to work to your family’s residency status. Real-World Consequences A visa mismatch creates immediate and serious problems that are difficult to fix once you’ve arrived. A remote worker enters on a Standard Work Visa, which requires a Spanish employer. When they try to continue working for their foreign company, they find it’s illegal. They should have applied for the Digital Nomad Visa and now face a complicated, costly process to switch categories. An entrepreneur gets a Digital Nomad Visa to work as a freelancer but then decides to register a Spanish limited company (S.L.). This action violates the visa’s terms, which are for remote work, not for founding a Spanish-based business. They risk having their residency canceled. Your visa isn’t a suggestion; it’s a legally binding framework for your life in Spain. Choosing the wrong one puts your residency, income, and future in the country at immediate risk. How to Get It Right from the Start Proactive planning based on your specific circumstances is the only way to avoid these visa-related pitfalls. Your income source and long-term goals dictate the correct path. Assess Your Income Source: Before applying, determine if your income is from a Spanish employer (Work Visa), a foreign remote employer or clients (Digital Nomad Visa), or passive sources like investments or pensions (Non-Lucrative Visa). Calculate Your Financial Proof: Each visa has a minimum income threshold. For the Non-Lucrative Visa (NLV), you need to prove passive funds of at least €28,800 annually for a single applicant (based on 400% of the IPREM). The Digital Nomad Visa requires proof of income over EUR2,850 per month. Plan for Business and Family: If your goal is to launch a tech-based company, apply for the Entrepreneur Visa from the beginning. If you’re bringing family, verify the dependent requirements for your chosen visa, as they differ significantly. Don’t assume your spouse automatically has the right to work. Choosing the right visa from the start saves immense stress and expense. If you’re considering a move but are unsure about your passive income eligibility, you can explore the requirements for Spain’s Non-Lucrative Visa here. Not sure which path fits? Book a consultation and we’ll map out the best option. 3. Missing Tax Obligations and Reporting Deadlines Many relocators seriously underestimate the complexity of the Spanish tax system. A common and costly mistake is assuming your foreign income is exempt or that you can simply continue as a non-resident indefinitely. Once you become a tax resident in Spain, you are obligated to report your worldwide income on the annual Declaración de la Renta. Missing key deadlines can trigger significant penalties, interest, and even investigations by the Agencia Tributaria, Spain’s tax agency. This isn’t a minor oversight. The Spanish tax system is rigorous, with strict reporting requirements for annual income, quarterly business returns, and foreign assets. Even beneficial regimes like the Beckham Law require precise, timely election and documentation to secure their tax advantages. Ignoring these rules is one of the most serious mistakes you can make when moving to Spain. Real-World Consequences The financial fallout from tax non-compliance is severe. We regularly assist clients who have fallen into these traps. A digital nomad earning €50,000 annually from foreign clients wrongly believed he could maintain non-resident status. After two years of not filing, he faced over €30,000 in accumulated penalties and back taxes. A remote employee who qualified for the Beckham Law failed to elect it within the 6-month deadline after their social security registration. This single error cost them over €50,000 in tax savings, as the exemption cannot be claimed retroactively. An expat with a foreign bank account over €50,000 failed to file the Modelo 720 (foreign asset declaration). They were hit with automatic penalties starting at €1,500 for late reporting. Misunderstanding your tax obligations creates immense financial risk. Simple reporting oversights can escalate into tens of thousands of euros in penalties, turning your Spanish dream into a bureaucratic nightmare. How to Get It Right from the Start Proactive tax management is essential from day one. Proper planning ensures you stay compliant and avoid costly errors. Elect Beckham Law Status Early: If you qualify, you must elect this special tax regime via Modelo 149 within six months of registering with Spanish social security. Know Your Deadlines: Set calendar reminders. The annual income tax return (Renta) is due between April and June. Quarterly VAT/IRPF returns for autónomos are due 20 days after each quarter ends. The foreign asset report (Modelo 720) is due by March 31st. Maintain Meticulous Records: Keep detailed records of all foreign income, expenses, and currency conversions. When planning your move, ensure you thoroughly research visa requirements and tax implications; a comprehensive resource like this guide on Working Remotely Abroad: A Practical Guide to Visas and Taxes can be very helpful. We specialize in Beckham Law planning, annual tax returns for residents and non-residents, and resolving penalties with the tax agency. Contact us for personalized advice to ensure your tax affairs are managed correctly from the start. 4. Delaying Healthcare and Social Security Registration A common and costly oversight for many moving to Spain is assuming healthcare is automatic or that their home country’s insurance will suffice indefinitely. New arrivals often delay registering with the Spanish National Health System (SNS) and Social Security, creating dangerous gaps in coverage. Access to Spain’s public healthcare is directly tied to your Social Security contributions or specific residency status; it is not a default entitlement. Delaying this process means you might only have access to emergency care, leaving you to cover routine doctor visits, specialist appointments, and prescription costs out-of-pocket. This is a significant mistake, as the SNS is the foundation for everything from maternity care to chronic condition management. Real-World Consequences These registration delays lead to very real and stressful financial and medical problems. In our experience, the consequences can be severe. A remote worker on a Digital Nomad Visa relies on their initial travel insurance, delaying their autónomo and Social Security registration. A sudden illness leads to hospitalization, resulting in an €8,000 bill that their basic insurance won’t cover. They also lose months of contributions towards their future Spanish pension. A spouse on a family reunification visa assumes they are automatically covered under their working partner’s healthcare. During her pregnancy, she discovers she must be registered separately as a beneficiary, causing significant delays in accessing prenatal care through the SNS. Missing your healthcare and Social Security registration creates immediate financial risk and long-term disadvantages. What seems like a low-priority admin task can leave you uninsured and ineligible for crucial state benefits when you need them most. How to Get It Right from the Start You can prevent these issues by treating healthcare registration as a top priority upon establishing your residency. Register with the SNS Promptly: Once you have your residency card (TIE) and empadronamiento (town hall registration), go to your local health center (centro de salud) to apply for your health card (tarjeta sanitaria). Do this within your first month. Integrate with Social Security: If you’re employed, your employer handles your Social Security registration. If you are self-employed (autónomo), you must register yourself with the Tesorería de la Seguridad Social (TGSS). This step activates your right to public healthcare. Understand Your Visa’s Requirements: For NLV holders, you must have comprehensive private health insurance for your first year. Afterwards, you may be able to join the public system via a special agreement (convenio especial). Always register your family members as dependents immediately upon their arrival. We coordinate healthcare and social security registration alongside your visa and residency applications, ensuring you have compliant coverage and access to benefits from day one. 5. Signing a Rental Contract Without Understanding Spanish Law Rushing to sign a rental agreement without a clear grasp of Spanish law is another of the biggest mistakes when moving to Spain. New arrivals often accept terms at face value, unaware that Spain’s Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos (Urban Leasing Law) heavily favors the tenant. This means your contract may have legal implications, like automatic renewals, that aren’t immediately obvious. It’s common for foreigners to sign informal or unregistered contracts, known as renting bajo mano (under the table). While it may seem easier or cheaper initially, this puts both you and the landlord at serious risk. The landlord is evading taxes, and you have no legal protection, making you vulnerable to sudden rent hikes, eviction, or loss of your deposit. Real-World Consequences We frequently see expats face preventable housing crises because they overlooked the details of their rental agreements. An expat signs a one-year lease, believing it’s a short-term commitment. They are shocked to discover the contract automatically renews for up to five years by law, unless they provide specific written notice two months before the end of the term. A couple rents a furnished flat with a verbal agreement. When the landlord decides to raise the rent by €200 mid-year, they have no formal contract to enforce the original price, leaving them with no legal recourse. A family rents an apartment bajo mano for a good price. They later find out the landlord has significant tax debts, and the property is seized by the Agencia Tributaria. The family faces an emergency eviction with no legal standing to fight it. An unvetted rental contract is a hidden liability. What seems like a quick solution can lead to legal disputes and the potential loss of your home and deposit. How to Get It Right from the Start Protect yourself by approaching any rental agreement with diligence and an awareness of your rights. Demand a Formal Contract: Always insist on a written contract (contrato de arrendamiento). Verbal agreements are difficult to enforce. The contract should clearly state the rent, term, and responsibilities of both parties. Verify the Landlord and Property: Ask the landlord for proof of ownership (nota simple) and confirm the property is legally registered for rental. This helps avoid scams and ensures the landlord is compliant, protecting you from tax-related evictions. Understand Your Rights: Familiarise yourself with Spain’s Urban Leasing Law. Key protections include the right to renew your contract for up to five years and limits on how much a landlord can increase the rent annually. Your deposit cannot exceed two months’ rent and should be placed in a regional government account. We advise on rental agreement legality as part of our comprehensive relocation support, ensuring your contract is fair and compliant before you sign. Contact us for personalized advice. 6. Postponing Your Business or Freelance (Autónomo) Registration Many entrepreneurs and freelancers moving to Spain wrongly assume they can operate informally or continue using foreign business structures indefinitely. Postponing registration as a self-employed worker (autónomo) or incorporating a Spanish company is a critical error. It’s not just an administrative formality; it’s a legal requirement that underpins your ability to work, invoice, and comply with Spanish law. Failing to register creates immediate and serious complications. You can’t legally invoice Spanish clients, which often means you can’t get paid. You also become ineligible for deducting business expenses and face significant penalties for unpaid social security contributions and tax non-compliance. The Spanish authorities do not permit retroactive registration to fix past mistakes; delays trigger automatic fines. Real-World Consequences These registration delays lead to stressful and costly outcomes. We see these scenarios frequently: A digital nomad freelancer operates for six months without autónomo registration, earning €15,000. When discovered, they face over €500 in late registration penalties, six months of back-dated social security contributions (at least €1,800), and are disqualified from deducting any business expenses from that period. A consultant earning over €40,000 annually works as an unregistered freelancer. When a major client requests an invoice with Spanish VAT (IVA), they discover they can’t legally provide one and lose the contract. A married couple, both freelancers, register separately as autónomos. They needlessly pay double social security costs, over €2,400 extra per year, because they were unaware of the autónomo colaborador (family assistant) status, which could have saved them over 50% on the second person’s contributions. Operating any business activity without proper registration in Spain isn’t a grey area; it’s a violation. The system is designed for immediate compliance, and delays result in financial penalties and an inability to conduct business legally. How to Get It Right from the Start You can avoid these business-killing mistakes with a proactive approach. The key is to register your business activity immediately upon starting. Register Promptly: You should register as an autónomo with both the tax agency (Agencia Tributaria) and Social Security (Tesorería General de la Seguridad Social) within 60 days of starting your activity in Spain. Gather Your Documents: Before starting, ensure you have your NIE, proof of address (empadronamiento), a Spanish bank account, and a clear description of your business activity to determine the correct tax codes. Evaluate Your Structure: For income under €40,000 per year, the autónomo structure is usually the simplest. For income consistently above €50,000, incorporating a limited company (Sociedad Limitada or SL) often becomes more tax-efficient. Bu

Close Service A1 Certificates - Social insurance in Europe From: Department of Social Protection Published on: 22 February 2024 Last updated on: 29 February 2024 What an A1 Certificate is Which country you pay social insurance in Who needs an A1 Certificate Apply for an A1 Certificate Contact us Operational guidelines What an A1 Certificate is An A1 Certificate is a document that confirms the country where a person pays their social insurance.If you are going to work in Europe for a short period of time for your employer, or as a self-employed worker, you need to apply for an A1 Certificate. The certificate can be valid for up to two years. Which country you pay social insurance in People usually pay social insurance in the country where they work. For example, if a person works in Ireland, they pay social insurance (PRSI) in Ireland.However, sometimes people work for Irish employers for short periods in Europe, or they can work in many countries as part of their duties.When work requires movement into other European countries, European Union law is used to decide the country where social insurance must be paid. Who needs an A1 Certificate Employed and self-employed people who are working in Europe may be asked to prove where they pay social insurance.To avoid confusion, all employees leaving Ireland to work in Europe for Irish employers, should have an A1 Certificate to cover their period of work abroad.All self-employed people who are leaving Ireland to work in Europe, should also have an A1 Certificate to cover their period of work abroad.When you get the A1 Certificate it will tell you where you should pay social insurance. That may be in Ireland, even though you are working abroad, or it may be in another country. Apply for an A1 Certificate If you are an employee, your employer should apply for an A1 Certificate at least four weeks before the start of your employment in Europe. If you are self-employed, you should apply for your A1 Certificate at least four weeks before the start of your work in Europe.You can apply online for an A1 Certificate on the Welfare Partners platform here.To get started on Welfare Partners, you must first register with Revenue for online services (ROS) certificate ROS Registration.After registering on ROS, you must also download a Department of Social Protection (DSP) sub-certificate from the ROS platform to allow you to log in on Welfare Partners. For information, see ROS Sub-Certificate Guide.After logging in on Welfare Partners, you can apply for an A1 Certificate by selecting the option “A1 Certificate application and company profile”. rows.content: ⚡ FREE TOOL: INSTANT NIE FORM GENERATOR • 🇪🇸 DOWNLOAD OFFICIAL EX-15 PDF • 📄 FILL IN ENGLISH, PRINT IN SPANISH ⚡ FREE TOOL: INSTANT NIE FORM GENERATOR • 🇪🇸 DOWNLOAD OFFICIAL EX-15 PDF • 📄 FILL IN ENGLISH, PRINT IN SPANISH Services Pricing Resources Calculator Blog & Guides Expat Glossary About Us Partner Program Contact ☀️ Book Free Call Official Guide Spanish Social Security Registration for Expats: From NIE to Seguridad Social 🗓️ November 2025 ⚖️ Vetted by JURO Legal Network ⚖️ Legal Transparency: This guide is authored by JURO Spain's relocation experts. We work alongside a vetted network of licensed Spanish attorneys for formal filings. This content is for informational purposes and does not constitute legal advice. Registering with Spain’s Tesorería General de la Seguridad Social (TGSS) is essential for accessing public healthcare, employment benefits, and pension contributions. This guide walks you through the documents, timelines, and online tools expats need to secure a Social Security number and attach it to their residency status. Table of contents Who needs a Spanish Social Security number Documents to prepare How to apply in person How to apply online with Cl@ve Linking healthcare and employment benefits Common issues and fixes FAQs Related guides Who needs a Spanish Social Security number You must obtain a Número de Seguridad Social (NUSS) if you: Start employment with a Spanish company or register as autónomo. Want to access the public healthcare system after relocating to Spain. Sponsor dependants for healthcare coverage or family benefits. Apply for maternity, paternity, or unemployment support. Non-EU residents usually complete this step immediately after receiving their NIE/TIE card. EU citizens can request the number before formal residency if they plan to work. Documents to prepare Gather digital and paper copies of: Passport and NIE/TIE card. Empadronamiento certificate issued within the last three months. Employment contract, autónomo registration (Modelo TA.0521), or university enrolment letter. Completed Modelo TA.1 application form. Social Security appointment confirmation (if applying in person). Translate foreign documents into Spanish and add apostilles where required by your provincial TGSS office. How to apply in person Book an appointment via the Cita Previa system on the Social Security website. Select Asignación Número Seguridad Social as the appointment type. Bring your TA.1 form, identification, and supporting documents. Submit them at the TGSS office; you’ll receive your NUSS on the spot or via email the same day. Tip: Arrive 15 minutes early to clear security and verify paperwork before your appointment window. How to apply online with Cl@ve Activate Cl@ve Permanente or obtain a digital certificate (certificado digital) from FNMT. Log into the TGSS portal and choose Alta en Seguridad Social. Upload scanned copies of your TA.1, ID, and padrón certificate. Submit the request; Social Security will issue your number via email, usually within 48 hours. If you lack Cl@ve credentials, request an in-person identity verification appointment at the Post Office or TGSS office to finish the registration. Linking healthcare and employment benefits After receiving your NUSS, notify your employer or file autónomo registration to activate contributions. Visit your local centro de salud with the Social Security certificate to request a Tarjeta Sanitaria Individual (TSI). Add dependants by submitting their documentation through the Import@ss portal or TGSS office. Update your data (address, phone, bank details) using Import@ss to keep records accurate for future benefits. Common issues and fixes Duplicate numbers: If you previously worked in Spain, request a certificate of affiliation instead of a new number. Missing padrón: Book empadronamiento quickly many TGSS offices reject applications without proof of residence. Expired passports: Renew before applying; TGSS will not issue a NUSS with an expired document. Appointment delays: Check nearby towns for faster availability or visit during early-morning walk-in slots. FAQs Can students get a Social Security number? Yes. Provide your enrolment letter and internship or part-time contract to justify the application. Do freelancers need a Social Security number before registering as autónomo? You can submit the TA.1 and TA.0521 forms together; TGSS assigns the number and finalises your autónomo enrolment in one visit. Will my NUSS expire if I leave Spain? No. The number is permanent. Reactivate contributions when you return or start a new job. EN - English FR - FrançaisEN - English Step You want to know the applicable deductibles when transferring your main residence in France ImprimerEnvoyer par emailPartager You transfer your main residence to France, and want to know the franchises you can benefit from. You can benefit from a duty and tax exemption for the import of your personal property. Goods admitted duty-free You come from a member country of the European Union When you move to France from a country in the European Union, there is no special customs formality to complete. You come from a non-EU country You can benefit from a duty and tax exemption for the import of your personal property, when you have been staying in a third country for at least 12 months and you wish to transfer your main residence to France. Your personal property used privately for at least 6 months before the transfer of residence is admitted free of charge, and acquired indifferently, all taxes included or excluding taxes. Please note: your personal belongings must have borne customs and/or tax charges in the country of origin or provenance to benefit from the exemption. Excluded from the exemption are alcoholic products, tobacco and tobacco products, means of transport of a commercial nature, mixed-use vehicles, transportable dwellings, equipment for professional use other than portable instruments for mechanical or liberal arts, stocks of raw materials and of worked or semi-worked products. Please note: Embassy staff and international organizations may be subject to different regimes and must approach the French Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs. Special case of the islands of St. Martin and St. Bartholomew: Sint Maarten is part of the customs territory of the European Union, but remains excluded from the fiscal territory of the EU. Saint Bartholomew has left the Community customs territory since 1 January 2012. Since neither customs duties, VAT nor dock dues are payable in these islands or on goods imported there, goods dispatched from these islands to another part of the customs territory of the EU are subject to the duties and taxes payable. Thus, if you previously resided in Saint-Martin or Saint-Barthélemy and you transfer your main residence to metropolitan France, your means of transport acquired on one of these two islands or imported into one of these two islands, will be subject to the duties and taxes in force (depending on their origin) when they are imported into metropolitan France. Details of imports of goods intended to furnish a secondary residence located in France or in the European Union Goods intended for the development of a second home are no longer allowed free of customs duties and VAT. You must pay the customs duty, VAT and any additional taxes on the entire move to your second home. For this purpose, you will have to provide the customs service with the exact list of imported goods and their value (presentation of invoices or estimate by mutual agreement with the service). The total declared value will be the basis for taxing your move (Customs value). You are also asked to produce the transport and insurance bill for your move. The rates and regulations for your goods and objects are based on the codification (tariff nomenclature) of the goods and the country of origin. The conditions to be fulfilled You must transfer your property to France within 12 months of the date of transfer of your residence. The importation of your goods can take place in one or more times. In the latter case, the inventory handed over to the customs service at the time of the first importation must take over all the goods for which exemption is claimed. You may not divest yourself (sale or lease, loan, pledge, etc.) of your goods admitted duty-free before a period of 12 months from their date of entry into France. The formalities to be carried out You must provide customs with the following documents: a detailed, estimated, dated and signed inventory (in 2 copies) of the effects and movable objects intended for importation; the cerfa 10070 declaration of entry into France free of charge of personal property from third countries, any document proving that: you had your principal residence in a third country; you settle in France (any document that can demonstrate the change of residence, transfer order for French military and civil servants or residence card, immigrant card, etc.). In return the customs gives you: a certified copy of the inventory; an 846 A certificate for the registration of your vehicle in a normal series; a free movement card drawn up, if applicable, at your request. Documents BOD - Customs and tax exemptions under ordinary import law BOD - Les franchises douanières et fiscales de droit commun à l'importation - ODT 1 Mo Infos Douane Service Nous vous renseignons sur les formalités douanières pour les particuliers et les professionnels. Preferences cookies Accept all the cookies Go to content Italian Government IT EN Header, social and menu of site Ambasciata d'Italia a Washington Sito ufficiale Ambasciata d'Italia a Washington Follow us: Ricerca sito live Search on site digita... Close Menu About usItaly & USAConsular Services and VisasNewsroom Search on site Search on site Home>Consular Services and Visas>Services for the Italian citizen>Registry of Italians Residing Abroad (AIRE)>Permanent Return to Italy – Customs Procedures Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on WhatsApp Share Share on Social Network Permanent Return to Italy – Customs Procedures Italian citizens registered with the AIRE (Registry of Italians Residing Abroad – Law 27.10.1988, no. 470) are entitled to customs exemption when they permanently return to Italy after residing continuously and permanently abroad for at least 12 months. All items to be imported into Italy for the permanent return must be owned and used by the applicant and must be intended for his or her exclusive personal use. The importation of goods under customs exemption for different purposes is prohibited. Household Goods (Masserizie) To obtain customs exemption, the Consulate does not need to isse any document in the case of importing only household goods. The Italian Customs Office requires: Repatriation self-declaration form showing the date of arrival abroad and that of the return to Italy, including the address or at least the municipality of the next residence, and the list of household goods (dishes, clothing, toys, etc.) Vehicles It is possible to import vehicles (cars, motorcycles, or other motorized movable objects) into Italy, only if they have been owned by the returning citizen for at least 6 months. You can submit a certification request to the Vital Records’ Office (stcivile.washington@esteri.it) by attaching copies of the following documentation: Repatriation self-declaration form for customs with vehicle Certificate of Title of the vehicle translated into Italian with an apostille (the apostille does not need to be translated) Vehicle registration Declaration or letter with the technical specifications of the motor vehicle issued by the seller (optional document) Declaration of conformity of the vehicle to CE regulations, only if issued by the dealer (optional document) All the above-mentioned documents must be submitted exclusively in ORIGINAL, with APOSTILLE, and accompanied by a TRANSLATION into Italian. For more information, please visit the website of the Italian Customs Agency. Repatriation with Pets If you are returning to Italy with a pet, you must follow these rules: The animals must be pets. It is not allowed to bring animals into Italy for commercial purposes using this type of service. Pets must be over three months old. Pets must travel with the owner or a person authorized by the owner. You may bring a maximum of five (5) pets, which can be dogs, cats, ferrets, or other animals, such as fish, frogs, turtles, and birds, as long as they do not belong to the protected category regulated by CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora). The introduction of pets is regulated by the European Union (see Regulation 998\2003\CE). For more information, visit the website of the Italian Ministry of Health. Required Documents Veterinary certificate to EU, filled out and signed by the Official Veterinary Service, containing information about the good health of the animal. Microchip or readable tattoo. Valid rabies vaccination certificate. The certificate does NOT need to be legalized by this Consular Chancellery; the signature of the veterinarian in the respective county or city is sufficient.
